General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Calif ↗ Open Full Page

Java4Shell: RCE in OpenJDK when processing Base64

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (960 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calif

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After we disclosed PHP2Shell, we realized many people didn't know what PHP was.
  • Today, we are disclosing Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder.
  • Industry observers note that while PHP is a high-level web technology, Java sits much deeper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After we disclosed PHP2Shell, we realized many people didn't know what PHP was. So we decided to go after something a little more familiar: Java.

Today, we are disclosing Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. OpenJDK is the most popular Java runtime. Under CVSS 4.0, this vulnerability scores 9.2 out of 10 (CRITICAL).

Industry observers note that while PHP is a high-level web technology, Java sits much deeper. Java is the world's third most popular programming language, powering 90% of Fortune 500 companies. It is the beating heart of the modern economy. Banking, aviation, telecommunications, nearly every critical sector runs on Java, including national security systems.

Base64 is a very common way of representing binary data as text. It is used in authentication protocols, to encode file uploads, and to deliver network messages. To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once. We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory. With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution. The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single =:.

In older OpenJDK 17, the trigger input is 128 of A followed by =.

Our initial testing demonstrated remote code execution in the following widely deployed Java applications, in their default configs.

Recent findings suggest that the lists are non-exhaustive. We also demonstrated RCE in sample applications built on widely used frameworks, including Apache Struts and Spring Boot. Ordinary features such as authentication and file uploads can expose the vulnerable Base64 decoder, extending the potential impact far beyond the products we tested. samczsun also shared a client-side exploit with us. A Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised, even if it exposes no service of its own.

Here are a demo video of the exploits running:.

In a recent development, memory corruption is the most common class of vulnerability on the Internet. But one of Java's biggest selling points is memory safety. Java manages memory on developers' behalf and checks memory accesses, protecting applications from the memory-corruption bugs common in other software.

But like PHP and many other technologies, much of Java itself is written in low-level languages like C, C++, and, in this case, assembly, where memory corruption is still a part of life.

It has been revealed that to speed up Base64 decoding, OpenJDK uses specialized AVX-512 VBMI instructions on supported x86-64 processors. The bug sits in the hand-rolled assembly code that handles the final few characters. For the 65-character input above, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte result array. After decoding the first 64 characters, the routine mishandles the stray = and calculates a negative output length. That invalid length becomes a full 64-byte write, sending 62 bytes past the end of the array. Java eventually rejects the input, but by then neighboring objects may already be corrupted.

As with PHP2Shell, Calif used AI to find and weaponize Java4Shell. AI brings the horsepower. Our researchers bring the context. The best hacker today is neither AI nor human. It is the centaur hacker, part human, part AI.

Recent findings suggest that it took our own Quang Luong an hour to discover the vulnerability, and two more hours to develop the first working exploit. The total token cost was less than $200.

One thing to note about this vulnerability is that there is no universal exploit. Depending on how Base64 is used and how the application works, different steps may be required for exploitation. Calif was able to accelerate the exploit development by spending initial effort building pipelines and strategies, then directing AI agents to use those for initial exploitation. Afterwards, most of the later chains are built almost autonomously with AI.

Java is one of many shared software stacks we all rely on. Over the years, it has grown to serve many different needs. Each feature request may make sense on its own, but everyone inherits the added complexity. Those who need a feature get the benefit. Everyone else carries the code and its risks, even if they never use it.

Java4Shell is a concrete example. The Base64 optimization helps applications that decode enormous amounts of data. But the code ships to everyone else too, including applications that gain little from it. On affected systems, an optimization few applications needed became a serious security risk.

Sources indicate that features can be useful, and most bugs can be fixed. But why do we have to worry about code we never needed in the first place?

If you don't need something, there is little reason to keep it running in your systems. Do you need that hand-rolled assembly Base64 decoder to process a few hundred bytes? Probably not.

Earlier this year we found Squidbleed, an older cousin of Heartbleed, hiding in the Squid proxy since 1997. The bug was in Squid's FTP module. But who uses FTP anymore? It's a dead protocol and should be removed.

Removing code is harder than it sounds. An apparently unused feature may have hidden dependencies. Someone has to understand what can be removed, make the change, and test what remains.

This is where AI can help to make that work practical at a scale we could not previously afford.

The same centaur hacker that discovered PHP2Shell and Java4Shell can comb a large codebase and flag dead code, bloated features, and needless optimizations. We call this vibe-uncoding: identify the parts a system actually needs, then remove everything else to reduce its attack surface.

With AI, everyone is asking, “What can we build?” But maybe the right question for security is, “What can we delete?”.

How to hide the new macOS 27.3 menu bar indicator

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (329 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, macOS 27.3 beta 2 adds a blue menu bar indicator for apps using System & App Protection Override.
  • In a recent development, if you regularly use trusted automation tools and utilities, that can mean a persistent pill taking up space in your menu bar.
  • I’ve tested this on macOS 27.3 beta 2 and confirmed that the indicator disappears after a restart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, macOS 27.3 beta 2 adds a blue menu bar indicator for apps using System & App Protection Override. Apple describes itas a transparency indicator that appears when one app is controlling another.

In a recent development, if you regularly use trusted automation tools and utilities, that can mean a persistent pill taking up space in your menu bar. Prefer to hide it? There’s a Terminal workaround.

I’ve tested this on macOS 27.3 beta 2 and confirmed that the indicator disappears after a restart.

Open Terminal and run these two commands:.

sudo mkdir -p /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domainsudo defaults write /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR -dict Enabled -bool false.

Enter your Mac administrator password when prompted, then restart your Mac.

The command disables the internal AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR feature flag. It doesn’t remove apps from your permissions list, although you’ll no longer see this activity indicator.

To restore Apple’s default behavior, run:.

sudo defaults delete /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR.

Restart your Mac again to apply the reversal. This removes only the indicator override, preserving any other flags you may have configured.

This is an undocumented workaround tested on the current beta, so Apple could change or remove it in a future update.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Cambridge Dictionary has named ‘human’ as the Word of the Year 2026.

The year has been defined by global debates on what it means to be human when AI is blurring the boundaries between people and machines.

'Human' is defined in the Cambridge Dictionary as ‘having the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines’.

In 2026, many public figures defended humans and humanity in the age of AI. Bill Gates, Chair of the Gates Foundation, made the case for “human reserved jobs”, such as caregivers, that should never be taken by machines, in a widely read essay.

According to recent reports, commenting on the selection of ‘human’ as Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year, he said: “AI is making us think harder about what it means to be human. It could help us cure diseases, improve education, and give people more time to spend on the things that matter most.

Industry observers note that "But we need to make deliberate choices about how it fits into our lives, including where we want people to remain at the center. The measure of AI’s success should be how much it improves human lives.”.

‘AI godfather’ and Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton has warned that “we’re creating alien beings. I’m willing to be selfish and choose humans.” And in his Magnifica Humanitas letter, Pope Leo XIV spoke of newly introduced forms of “dehumanization” and the “pressing duty to remain profoundly human”.

Actors Scarlett Johansson and Cate Blanchett, musicians Tayla Parx, LeAnn Rimes and Billie Eilish, and authors Jodi Picoult and Jonathan Franzen challenged an "assault on human creativity" as the Human Artistry Campaign and Artist Rights Alliance opposed machine-generated replicas and theft of human-generated content by large language models (LLMs).

Meanwhile, Project Hail Mary author Andy Weir has wondered whether he "might be among the last generation of fully human writers". The Authors Guild has rolled out a ‘Human Authored’ kitemark for books, supported by Professor Dame Mary Beard and Malorie Blackman.

As AI deepfakes simulated humans, Matthew McConaughey became the first Hollywood actor to pre-emptively protect himself against unauthorised digital reproduction by trademarking clips of his voice, his face and even his catchphrase ‘alright, alright, alright’. Taylor Swift followed suit, trademarking her voice and image in April.

Professor Rachel Adams, an expert on AI governance and human rights at the University of Cambridge, noted: “AI brings us back to questions that we’ve asked for millennia: who are we, what does it mean to be human? The answer to these questions has never been fixed or stable, but the act of asking it is something we have in common.

Recent findings suggest that “AI is going to be a profound test for humanity. There’s a real risk that it deepens existing inequalities, but it also has the potential to solve them.".

Dr Tom McClelland, a philosopher of science at the University of Cambridge, stated: “I think ‘human’ is a really interesting choice because right now our understanding of humanity is changing.

According to recent reports, “We're trying to understand the difference between a human mind and an artificial mind, between living beings like us and artificial beings that we're creating. What sets us apart, is it consciousness, creativity or compassion?

“All the rhetoric around AI is about what's inevitably going to happen. But to young people growing up in an AI-enabled world, my advice would be that nothing is inevitable. What happens in the future of AI is up to us. It's up to you.".

According to recent reports, lexicographer Colin McIntosh of the Cambridge Dictionary stated: “AI is changing how we talk about being human. It’s this renewed interest in the idea of being human that captured the zeitgeist and made ‘human’ the Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year.”.

Adapted from the Cambridge University Press & Assessment website.

#27578. A Perfect SimCity

A Perfect SimCity

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1401 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jeffquast

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After 35 years of playing SimCity, I still could not say what makes a "Perfect" city.
  • It has been revealed that don Hopkins has been maintaining FOSS ports of SimCity (1989) as Micropolis and MicropolisCore, faithfully reproducing the ruleset of the original.
  • According to recent reports, the population of a perfectly scoring city is 12-16k.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After 35 years of playing SimCity, I still could not say what makes a "Perfect" city. An evaluation screen displays a Score of 0 to 1000, and I struggled to reach 900 and never understood its factors. Discovering these factors by play is the fun of a simulation game, and this one has the advantage that the source code is also available.

It has been revealed that don Hopkins has been maintaining FOSS ports of SimCity (1989) as Micropolis and MicropolisCore, faithfully reproducing the ruleset of the original. Using the Python shims provided by gym-city I have run many experiments and share these results here, presenting five high-scoring and five high-population cities, designed algorithmically using the strategies shared below.

According to recent reports, the population of a perfectly scoring city is 12-16k. Their population level, crime rate, pollution and land value are perfectly balanced to sustain a 1% Tax Rate. Their roads and rails are few and non-contiguous. A perfectly scoring city is without any fire department, and bigscore2 through 5 have no police station.

Industry observers note that travel requirements of residential and industrial zones are simple. They check their twelve surrounding tiles for any road or rail to decide if it should grow. If none is there, the zone declines.

Recent findings suggest that commercial zones require a delivery, a vehicle starts on the perimeter road and walks up to 30 steps, arriving the moment it stands beside a developed tile. The zone's own tiles count, so any loop of track under 30 steps satisfies it. Commercial zones are placed in the city center because the engine provides a downtown bonus, starting at +64 and falling off to a -64 penalty in the far corners of the map.

The PC SimCity manual recommends rails and it is the most obvious strategy that players discover on their own. Roads carry traffic and emit pollution, which suppresses residential growth. Rails emit no pollution and register no traffic at all.

Recent findings suggest that roads and rails incur an annual cost, and Police and Fire are very large budget items, they severely impact score if they are under-funded and so must be at 100% funding. Having neither departments is the lowest annual cost allowing for the lowest Tax Rate. Raising the Tax Rate to 2% lowers the score almost 30 points, through direct and indirect factors.

In the Super Nintendo edition the game rewards population, the final reward of Megapolis is issued at a population of 500k. Casual players report cities of 600k to 700k on the SNES platform, with one player reporting 911.2k.

It has been revealed that 911.2k is probably out of reach for Micropolis. The Super Nintendo is the only edition to offer gifts, which increase land value when placed, allowing for higher zone density in the areas outside of the downtown bonus.

I have also experimented with optimizing for population by algorithm, and I am able to reach 700k by automatic code.

Score is calculated in two stages, the first uses seven penalty terms:.

Figure 2. The seven scoring terms. Six are bounded at zero and can only subtract, and traffic can be as high as 576. Unemployment has no lower bound, a negative value raises score.

According to recent reports, six out of seven terms are bounded at zero. However, unemployment is unbounded:.

Sources indicate that when the number of jobs exceeds the residents zoned to fill them, The Unemployment term goes negative and adds to the score, providing a score bonus of about 128 points. No other term moves the score this much.

The second stage of score calculation is reduction by nine more penalties:.

According to recent reports, figure 3. Each penalty applies to what the one above it left, so the same factor is worth less further down the list. The right-hand column is what each costs a city scoring 940.

The first three are penalties for failing to build a special zone. Surpassing 500 residents demands a stadium, 100 commercial an airport and 70 industrial a seaport. Where a stadium is placed does not matter to score, having no traffic or pollution. However, Airports and Seaports do reduce overall score, because of their high-density pollution and so they are not built.

Industry observers note that each of those seven penalty terms is an average, and the land value scan.cpp decides what is included by each 2x2 square of map by their tile ID. Grass, forest and park trees are under 64 and invisible to scoring, but a fountain of ID 840 includes it for grading, even though nobody lives in it!

These 2x2 squares otherwise carry no population, pulling down the crime penalty term by 33 points.

Figure 5. A 2x2 square is counted only when it contains tile ID 64 or greater, while land value is credited only from tile IDs below 44. The park building tool has a one in five chance to draw a fountain, ID 840. Placing fountains lower total crime penalty.

Many guides recommend parks to reduce or absorb pollution, but they do not reduce pollution at all in Micropolis. However, pollution reduces land value, and land value drives crime, so parks lower crime indirectly by raising the land value around them.

Water, park and tree tiles all increase land value, and the engine counts them in 4x4 blocks. Every such tile credits its block 15 points, and the final credit to land value is this sum, plus downtown bonus, minus pollution.

However, this land value credit is kept as a single byte, and smoothTerrain() in scan.cpp blends a block with its neighbors before it divides, so a block with its surroundings may sum beyond 255 and wrap around, counter-intuitively lowering land value.

Figure 4. Number of Water, park or tree tiles in a 4x4 block against the land value it credits. Exactly 1/2 of the tiles (8) is the optimal value of greenery. At 9 of 16 tiles, it is in danger of driving down land value when summed with its neighbors.

Sources indicate that the PC SimCity manual declares that "Parks, like forests and water, raise the land value of surrounding zones". However, too many parks or trees can push push down land value and increase crime.

According to recent reports, common strategy is to lay industrial zones by map edges, and this is recommended to maximize for population. The SNES SimCity manual writes, "One of the great benefits of building industrial Zones along the edges is that half the pollution is off the map and doesn't affect the city. This is very important when it comes to heavily polluting industries, Airports and Coal Power Stations.".

Industry observers note that this is partly true. The Micropolis engine spreads pollution outward from each source, divides the map into 4x4 blocks, and then creates an average of only the blocks that contain pollution:.

Tiles that contain low levels of pollution help bring down total pollution by this averaging, a small high-scoring city should keep the light density pollution for itself. Models suggest that a city maximized for population should place industrial zones on map edges for other reasons, that the land value there is too low to for other kind of zones.

It has been revealed that jay Wright Forrester's Urban Dynamics (1969) is often cited as an influence on Will Wright, Chief Designer of SimCity (1989). Urban Dynamics is essentially a paperback simulation of cities. The Micropolis simulation is vaguely recognizable as a minified version of the model in Urban Dynamics along with some small improvements in including spatial values of neighboring tiles that Forrester's models lack. Interestingly, both arrive at the same place: what improves a city most is reducing available housing:.

Sources indicate that the concurrent reduction of excess housing is absolutely essential. It supplies the land for new job-creating structures. Equally key, the resulting housing shortage creates the population-stabilizing pressure that allows economic revival to proceed without being inundated by rising population.

—Jay Forrester, Counterintuitive Behavior of Social Systems, 1971.

Sources indicate that the Sumerian Game (1963), considered the antecedent of the city-building game genre, contains the same anti-pattern, where I found the best strategy is systemic starvation of 3% of the population. I think in 2026 it would be difficult to find a proponent for the housing and population shortages that all three of these models suggest optimizing towards.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that according to OpenAI’s announcement, the firm’s newest frontier model can build more attractive, functional websites from a written description.
  • It has been revealed that as a working mom of three, I immediately thought of something I could actually use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I’ve tested plenty of AI tools that promise to make life easier, but I usually end up spending more time figuring out how to use them than I save. That’s why one particular feature of OpenAI’s upcoming GPT-6.2 Astra caught my attention.

It has been revealed that according to OpenAI’s announcement, the firm’s newest frontier model can build more attractive, functional websites from a written description. You don’t need to know how to code, design a website, or understand what happens behind the scenes.

It has been revealed that as a working mom of three, I immediately thought of something I could actually use. Between school schedules, activities, dinner plans and the endless list of things everyone needs to remember, keeping a family organized can feel like a full-time job.

So I decided to give GPT-6.2 Astra a single prompt and see whether it could build a family command center to keep everything in one place.

Industry observers note that my goal wasn’t to create another pretty dashboard. I wanted a website where I could move things around on a calendar, plan dinners, automatically generate grocery lists, and track chores without jumping between apps.

And I wanted ChatGPT to build the entire thing without asking me a dozen follow-up questions.

OpenAI introduced GPT-6.2 Astra on Tuesday, alongside GPT-6.2 Sol, a faster, more efficient model designed for everyday tasks.

Astra is the more powerful of the two, with improvements in coding, visual design and complex projects that require multiple steps.

One of the more interesting claims is that the model can create websites that not only look better but actually work better. OpenAI states Astra has improved visual reasoning, helping it choose layouts, images and interactive elements that fit the purpose of a website.

This matters because building something useful takes more than generating a page with a few buttons. Those buttons need to work, information needs to update correctly, and the experience should make sense to someone who isn’t a developer.

For this test, I wanted to see how close Astra could get to a finished website using nothing more than one detailed prompt.

I opened ChatGPT Work, selected GPT-6.2 Astra and entered the following prompt:.

Build me a fully functional, interactive family command center website that helps a busy household with three children stay organized.

I want a weekly calendar where I can add, edit and move events, including school activities, appointments and family prepares.

Sources indicate that include a meal planner for breakfast, lunch and dinner that automatically generates a grocery list based on the meals I select. Let me check off grocery items as I shop.

Add a chore tracker where I can assign tasks to different family members, mark them complete and see everyone's progress throughout the week.

Create a homepage dashboard showing today's events, upcoming activities, tonight's dinner and anything that still needs to get done.

Industry observers note that make the website beautiful, modern, mobile-friendly and simple enough for children and adults to use. Use realistic sample data so I can test everything immediately.

Every button, calendar interaction, checkbox and calculation must function. I don't want a static mockup.

Store changes so my information doesn't disappear when I refresh the page, if the available environment supports persistent storage.

According to recent reports, do not ask follow-up questions. Make reasonable design decisions yourself and build the complete experience.

In a recent development, before finishing, check the functionality, test the interactions and fix any problems you find. Tell me what you were unable to verify.

I deliberately included several features that depend on one another. A meal planner is useful on its own, but it becomes much more interesting when the meals automatically populate a grocery list.

I also wanted to see whether Astra could handle the less glamorous parts of building a website, such as saving changes and making sure everything still worked when I returned.

It has been revealed that as Astra worked, it kept me updated on its progress with responses like, "I’ll build a complete family organizer with a shared calendar, meal planning and grocery lists, chore tracking, and a dashboard, then test the main interactions and saved data."And then it went on to say, "The design is taking shape as 'Hearth,' with a calm dashboard and a color for each family member. I’m connecting the calendar, meal planner, grocery quantities, and weekly chore progress so changes carry through the whole app.At any time I could have interrupted the model and suggested it go a different way. For instance, if instead of a calm theme, I could have had it use bold or even neon colors to reflect the chaos of a home with three young children. Of course, I stayed with calm. Every little bit helps. It's crucial to note, if you're going to ask GPT-6.2 to create a website, it isn't as fast as Gemini Hydrogen. That's not because it's not as good or not working correctly, each model just works differently, and that includes latency. After 11 minutes, I asked, "Are you almost done?" It then responded with, "The visual layout is ready, and I’m finishing the interactive features. I still need to test adding and moving events, generating groceries, checking off chores, and saving through a refresh before it’s ready to use."When it finally completed the task, a beautiful, fully functional website in the browser appeared. I was truly surprised by how nice the website turned out.

Astra built a site that handles multiple connected tasks, remembers my changes and works without constant troubleshooting, that's a much more compelling demonstration of what AI can do than another chatbot answering questions.

GPT-6.2 Astra is available through ChatGPT Work for eligible Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu people, with access depending on the rollout and workspace permissions. The model is not being added to the regular Chat model selector as part of this launch.

To try it, open ChatGPT Work, select GPT-6.2 Astra if it's available and paste in the prompt above. You can customize it for your own household, changing the number of family members or adding features you'd find more useful.

You can also adapt the same approach to build a vacation planner, homework tracker, personal budget dashboard or other simple web app.

It has been revealed that the best way to judge the result is to try using it. Give it a try and let me know in the comments what you think.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • More than that, VSCO Studio Pro integrates with the company’s broader ecosystem of photography tools, allowing owners to manage their workflow from importing and editing photos to delivering finished images to clients through VSCO Galleries, without having to manually export and upload them to another app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

VSCO today released Studio Pro Desktop, its first native photo editor for Mac, bringing many of the manufacturer’s familiar editing tools to macOS, alongside upcoming features aimed at photographers working with large numbers of images. Here are the details.

Professional and amateur photographers just got a newly introduced alternative for editing and managing their photos on Mac with the release of VSCO Studio Pro, a native macOS app that brings the manufacturer’s popular editing tools to the desktop for the first time.

More than that, VSCO Studio Pro integrates with the company’s broader ecosystem of photography tools, allowing owners to manage their workflow from importing and editing photos to delivering finished images to clients through VSCO Galleries, without having to manually export and upload them to another app.

It also supports keyboard shortcuts similar to those found in other popular photo editors, making it easier for photographers familiar with those apps to get started.

Here’s Eric Wittman, CEO of VSCO, on today’s launch:.

“Photographers deserve tools built around how they actually work. […] 75% of VSCO Pro members have used our presets in the last six months. Now those looks live on the desktop, with one connected workflow from camera to client delivery and nothing getting in the way.

The first thing owners will notice, and then continue to notice when using VSCO Studio Pro, is how fast it is. From changing the grid size, to sorting images, to applying presets by rolling the cursor over each of the 200+ presets, pretty much everything about VSCO Studio Pro feels as real-time and instant as it can be when dealing with large numbers of images.

As for importing photos, VSCO Studio Pro supports Apple Photos, local folders, SD cards, and external drives, and offers RAW compatibility with more than 800 cameras from 20 brands. Users can also choose whether to work with files in their original location or copy them elsewhere.

Under the hood, VSCO Studio Pro Desktop combines Apple’s Core Image RAW processing with the company’s own Reflex image processing engine, which handles presets and editing adjustments.

Batch editing in VSCO Studio Pro Desktop can handle anywhere from two to 500 images at once, which is great for rapidly applying the same preset or film-inspired look (including Kodak Portra, Kodachrome, Fujifilm Velvia, and Kodak Tri-X), or making adjustments to an entire set of photos simultaneously, with changes appearing across all selected images in real time.

It has been revealed that and speaking of presets, VSCO Studio Pro packs an exclusive one called IOE1 Pro, developed with photographer Joe Greer. IOE1 Pro, as well as VSCO’s other presets, allow people to adjust the strength, color, tone, and contrast, further helping them fine-tune each look to their liking.

VSCO Studio Pro’s editing tools include the usual suspects photographers might expect from photo editing software, including exposure, contrast, fade, highlights, shadows, whites, blacks, skin tone, temperature, tint, hue, saturation, lightness, sharpening, clarity, vignetting, and grain adjustments for strength, size, and color.

VSCO is also working to expand its toolset to include bloom and halation effects, curves, masks, and a remove tool for users looking for more control over their edits and to make more precise, localized adjustments to their images.

Also in the works are newly introduced organizational features, including projects for managing groups of photos, as well as culling tools that will allow users to rate images with stars and mark them as accepted or rejected, making it easier to sort through large photo collections.

Sources indicate that once people are happy with their adjustments, they can export their photos individually or in batches, choosing the file name, format, resolution, and compression quality. VSCO Studio Pro also offers resizing presets for web, social media, and client delivery, as well as the option to save the finished images to a folder of their choice.

And speaking of client delivery, consumers can publish their edited photos directly to VSCO Galleries, allowing them to share full-resolution images without having to export them and upload them separately elsewhere.

VSCO Studio Pro Desktop is available today as a free download for Apple Silicon Macs, with full feature access requiring a VSCO Pro membership, starting at $4.99 per month or $59.99 per year, or a VSCO One membership. You can see it in action below:.

To learn more about VSCO Studio Pro Desktop, follow this link.

#27573. Tech Report: Energy-Based Reasoners: 385x more efficient inference

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (531 w)

Tech Report: Energy-Based Reasoners: 385x more efficient inference

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (531 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that looping is a powerful inductive bias for reasoning.
  • Existing looped reasoners upgrade their latent state without any explicit assessment of it.
  • The energy rates the compatibility between the reasoning state z and the initial board x.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that looping is a powerful inductive bias for reasoning. By repeatedly iterating a recurrent block, looped models can scale their effective depth and enable multi-step reasoning in latent space. However, existing looped models are not inherently guided by an explicit measure of progress, making it difficult to determine when to stop looping and how to improve upon the current state. To enable this, we introduce Energy-Based Reasoners (EBRs), which learn an energy function over latent reasoning states and formulate looped updates as gradient descent on this energy. The energy scores latent states, while its gradient guides refinement and provides a signal for stopping. To train EBRs effectively, we further introduce exploration-based training to discover additional modes and to better shape the energy landscape over a broader set of states. Across four algorithmic reasoning benchmarks, EBRs match or outperform prior recurrent reasoning models, achieving 99.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme while using 345× less inference compute than the next-best model and maintaining comparable training compute. On all multi-solution benchmarks, EBRs achieve state-of-the-art coverage of distinct valid solutions while maintaining near-100% single-sample accuracy. These results suggest that energy-based models are a promising approach for strong reasoning performance.

Existing looped reasoners upgrade their latent state without any explicit assessment of it. An EBR learns an energy function that guides refinement, stopping and selection.

Sources indicate that score. The energy rates the compatibility between the reasoning state z and the initial board x. Lower means better compatibility.

Refine. The gradient turns the score into an improvement direction.

Sources indicate that stop. The state becomes stationary once the gradient is small, so the gradient acts as a stopping criterion.

Recent findings suggest that select. Among multiple candidate solutions, we pick the one with the lowest energy.

According to recent reports, correct solutions settle at low-energy stationary states. Energy, gradient norm and step size during descent on Sudoku-Extreme. Correct trajectories settle at low energy with small gradients, while wrong ones keep moving.

Running more descent steps refines each answer further, and running more trajectories gives the energy more candidates to choose the lowest-energy one from.

EBRs reach EqR's best accuracy with 7× fewer iterations (left) and 43× fewer samples (right).

GRAM and TRM from GRAM's paper; EqR from its released checkpoint. Mean ± SD over three seeds.

Each trajectory stops once its energy gradient falls below a threshold, so easy puzzles finish in a few steps and hard ones keep going.

According to recent reports, EBRs give the best single-sample accuracy among reasoning models. Within only 5 passes, they reach 99.9% and 88.3%, ahead of methods that draw up to 128. Stopping each trajectory once its energy gradient falls below a threshold keeps 99.9% accuracy with 10.9× fewer FLOPs than a fixed-depth EBR, allowing us to surpass EqR with 345× fewer FLOPs.

EBR acts like stochastic gradient descent and can capture many different solutions. Coverage captures the share of each input's distinct valid solutions that 20 samples find.

Recent findings suggest that pass@1 (%) and Conflicts (edges summed over the test graphs) use one sample. Cov@20 is the share of distinct valid solutions found by 20 samples (%). Baselines from GRAM's paper.

Colette Kress, Nvidia’s interim chief executive and chief financial officer.

vidia’s board will not bring back Jensen Huang as chief executive, interim CEO Colette Kress mentioned on Tuesday. But support for his return is growing among some staff, CNBC reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

“The board has determined that they will not reinstate Jensen,” Kress told CNBC’s Jim Cramer on Mad Money.

Board chair Harvey Jones made the same point in his opening remarks on Nvidia’s earnings call earlier that day.

“The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Jones said.

In a recent development, huang noted on Tuesday, in his first public statement since resigning, that he would be willing to return. He had already discussed a possible return, the Financial Times reported. President Donald Trump has also said he would not object.

Inside the company, engineers in particular were deeply devoted to Huang, a former employee told CNBC. TNW has not independently verified CNBC’s reporting on staff sentiment.

Kress, who has been Nvidia’s finance chief since 2013, used her first earnings call as interim CEO to turn attention back to the business. She told Cramer that Nvidia’s customers and employees are staying with the company.

“We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners, they’re all 100% behind us,” Kress said on the call.

It has been revealed that the results helped. Revenue for the third quarter more than doubled to $115.8bn, ahead of analyst forecasts of about $109bn. Adjusted earnings came in at $2.68 a share.

Recent findings suggest that nvidia forecast record fourth-quarter revenue of about $130bn. Kress also raised the company’s revenue growth target for fiscal 2028 to 75%, from the 70% Huang gave three months ago. Nvidia added $150bn to its share buyback blueprint.

The shares rose about 3.5% in premarket trading on Wednesday, after falling for four days in a row, CNBC reported.

Separately, Kress mentioned Nvidia is no longer shipping licensed Hopper data centre chips to China, Bloomberg reported.

According to recent reports, huang resigned last week after admitting an affair with Alice Huang, whom US officials suspect of being a Chinese spy. He is due to appear before House panels on 1 December.

GTA 6 proves Rockstar still owns the cultural spotlight, but its next move shouldn’t take 10 years

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (696 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There is an unmistakable electricity around GTA 6.
  • In fact, it is easily the biggest pop-culture event in recent memory, and, arguably, of the 2000s.
  • Industry observers note that I love seeing a single game launch bring the entire entertainment world to a standstill.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is an unmistakable electricity around GTA 6. We live in an era where everyone’s feeds and watchlists are split across a thousand different niches, yet Rockstar’s return to Vice City has united everyone’s attention in a way I haven't felt in years.

In fact, it is easily the biggest pop-culture event in recent memory, and, arguably, of the 2000s.

Industry observers note that I love seeing a single game launch bring the entire entertainment world to a standstill. Yet beneath all that excitement lies a nagging catch: given how long Rockstar takes to build these worlds, once the credits roll we could easily be waiting until the mid-2030s for the studio's next massive release.

Instead of chasing another decade long mega project, what I want next from Rockstar is smaller, tighter stories.

Part of what makes GTA 6 so exciting has nothing to do with map size or frame rates, it's the thrill of everyone playing the exact same game at the exact same time. Years ago, massive launches were cultural earthquakes, with players swapping secrets at work or school the next morning and experiencing a story together.

Industry observers note that many games of today don't operate the same way, even if there's collective hype. Whether you game every night or haven't touched a controller in years, Vice City feels unmissable — which only makes waiting a decade between Rockstar releases feel even harder.

It has been revealed that people usually talk about Rockstar in terms of sheer size, from massive maps to sprawling online modes. Yet looking back at the studio’s catalogue, its greatest strength has always been capturing a specific time and place.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Nobody touches Rockstar when it comes to period detail. Red Dead Redemption 2 built a tactile portrait of 1899 America. Years earlier, the Rockstar-published, Team Bondi-developed L.A. Noire delivered a moody 1947 detective thriller where reading faces and cruising post-war Los Angeles felt completely unmatched.

Even the controversial Bully endures as a beloved classic precisely because its tight, atmospheric boarding school setting, memorable characters, and lived-in routines felt so convincing. Those games prove that what really pulls me into a Rockstar world is historical authenticity, not square mileage.

If every new Rockstar project has to out-scale GTA 6, we might only see two or three more games from the studio in our lifetimes, and that feels like a huge missed opportunity.

Recent findings suggest that once GTA 6 has its moment, I don't want Rockstar vanishing into another 10-year bunker to build GTA 7, although I am waiting on tenterhooks for Red Dead Redemption 3. Instead, I'd love to see the studio carve out space for tighter, 15-25 hour games in the spirit of L.A. Noire.

Recent findings suggest that just imagine what Rockstar’s writers could do with a gritty 1970s New York crime drama like The French Connection, a 1920s Prohibition bootlegging story, or even bring its storytelling back to its UK roots with a 1960s London drama set inside the era's booming fashion and rock-and-roll scene. The possibilities really are endless.

In a recent development, GTA 6 proves that Rockstar still owns the cultural spotlight like nobody else. Giving us smaller games between its mega-blockbusters wouldn't dilute that magic, but it would let us experience it more than once a decade.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI kicked off the GPT-6 generation with Astra in September, then upgraded Sol to GPT-6.1 a few weeks later at DevDay.

It has been revealed that today, GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol are coming to ChatGPT Work and Codex together. OpenAI indicates both can finish demanding tasks with fewer output tokens, so you can get more done before hitting your usage limit.

Astra is still the model OpenAI recommends for your hardest projects.

Say you have a screenshot of a slide and want the rest of your presentation to look like it. OpenAI notes GPT-6.2 Astra can use that screenshot as a template and match the layout, colors, and even the font size.

On the Codex side, OpenAI says Astra is better at making and testing changes in an existing project.

“Early testers reported cleaner code style and more focused tests, with fewer rounds of revision,” OpenAI states.

Sol is the more affordable model for everyday coding and writing, and it gets surprisingly close to Astra on one coding test.

Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0 measures whether changes to real codebases are good enough for maintainers to merge.

With both models at maximum reasoning effort, OpenAI says Sol came within half a point of Astra at about one-fifth the cost.

each::labs co-founders Eftal Yurtseven and Canberk Sinangil.

Generative media platform each::labs has raised a $7M seed round, the firm confirmed today, with Revo Capital and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) co-leading the investment.

Sources indicate that the San Francisco startup, founded in June 2024 by engineers from Türkiye, notes monthly revenue grew about fivefold between August and October, to roughly $2M. That puts its annualised run rate above $20mn, built on less than $2mn of earlier funding and a team of about 20 people.

According to recent reports, its platform puts over 600 outside models for images, video, and audio behind one API, next to models each::labs trains itself. Customers range from production studios and online retailers to consumer AI apps and ad platforms. More than 750 paid customers used the service in October, according to the company.

The growth followed a July rebuild aimed at reliability, and the firm states that when it replayed old customer traffic through the new system, the success rate went from 56% to 100%. Core requests also got up to 25 times faster, and a failed generation now falls back to another model on its own.

Usage then surged in September, as consumer AI apps moved into video, and the platform handled around a million daily runs in October, each::labs remarked. Character swapping became one of its heaviest workloads, prompting the team to build Lockstep, a model that keeps a clip’s motion while replacing who appears in it.

Lockstep debuted on 28 October at $0.09 per second of 720p video. The company indicates that is about a quarter of what Higgsfield’s rival Genjutsu Motion Transfer costs for the same resolution on its own marketplace. Ad firm Wask, meanwhile, uses the platform for its AI creative feature, generating over 1,000 ad creatives a minute at peak.

“Before generative media, if you couldn’t draw, you couldn’t show anyone what was in your head. Now you can, but only after fighting the tool for it,” stated Eftal Yurtseven, co-founder and CEO of each::labs. “We exist to close that gap. We build the layer above the models, and when the model our customers need doesn’t exist, we build it.”.

It has been revealed that yurtseven ran the data platform team at grocery delivery firm Getir before starting the tech giant with a fellow ex-Insider engineer. In October, each::labs also opened each::studio, a San Francisco space where film, VFX, and marketing teams use generative media without writing code.

Revo Capital, Türkiye’s largest early-stage fund, first invested in the startup in September 2025, and the EBRD anchors Revo’s $100mn third fund.

Industry observers note that the new capital will go towards more in-house models, sales and marketing hires in San Francisco, and a bigger each::studio. Its first outside round, in February 2025, was led by Right Side Capital.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.What You Will Learn:How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processesHow baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affectedHow in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structuresWhen offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign materialHow correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projectsRegister now for this free webinar!

In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar demonstrates how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.

In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session highlights how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

In a recent development, in the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also reveals how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Now that I’ve seen the Slate Truck in person and been inside the $25,000 electric pickup truck, I’m itching to take it out on the road for a proper test drive. In order for Slate to hit that price point, the tech giant stripped the cabin back to the basics — with practically everything being a manual affair. That means crank windows and manual seats, just to name a couple.

According to recent reports, even more surprising is the clutter-free dashboard, which ditches the massive center infotainment touchscreens I often see in the best electric cars and opts for a simple built-in phone mount. While I appreciate the distraction-free philosophy, going without a proper display for navigation is a tough adjustment for daily driving. That’s exactly where the CarpodGo T4 Plus — which offers seamless CarPlay and Android Auto support — comes in to save the day.

In a recent development, honestly, if you intend to buy the Slate Truck, it’s easily the first upgrade I’d recommend getting. Here’s why.

In a recent development, the CarpodGo T4 Plus adds a 10.9-inch, 1,000-nit touchscreen to any vehicle with zero permanent wiring, giving you smooth 60fps wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto in minutes. Its magnetic quick-release base lets you snap the display off when you park without unplugging cables, while Display Only Bluetooth Mode routes audio straight to your speakers. Don't forget to click the coupon to drop the price down to $229. If you're looking for something smaller, there's also the CarpodGo T4 with an 8.9-inch touchscreen.

One of the biggest reasons why I recommend the CarpodGo T4 Plus is that installing it is a breeze. In fact, I’d say it’s just as easy as setting up a dashcam — only much quicker. And the best part? It requires zero permanent dashboard modifications or wiring.

In a recent development, while the Slate Truck appears to tuck its 12V DC outlet inside the frunk rather than the cabin, I was able to power the display directly via USB-C in a Mazda CX-30, making it an easy plug-and-play fit for the Slate Truck's interior USB ports. The setup required me to attach the included fixed console mount onto a flat surface on the dash, plug in the power cable, and snap the screen onto the magnetic quick-release base.

Since the power runs straight through the base's pogo-pin connection, I’m able to lift the 10.9-inch screen right off whenever I park without fumbling with dangling cords. In my opinion, its plug-and-play experience perfectly suits the Slate Truck and its minimalist dashboard above.

Once powered on, the 10.9-inch, fully laminated IPS touchscreen gives me plenty of room for split-screen navigation and media controls — something I wouldn’t get from a phone clipped to the dash.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Having wireless access to both Apple CarPlay and Android Auto makes the CarpodGo T4 Plus the ultimate solution for the Slate Truck's barren cabin. Instead of juggling a phone mount for turn-by-turn directions, you get the familiar, driver-friendly interface of Google Maps (complete with the fresh Immersive Navigation experience), Apple Maps, Spotify, and hands-free messaging right on a wide touchscreen — running at a smooth 60 fps, so swiping and zooming feel genuinely responsive.

Sources indicate that even better is how flexible it is when it comes to handling audio, especially since the Slate Truck doesn’t come with any factory-installed speakers. Out of the box, the CarpodGo T4 Plus can output audio directly through its own built-in speaker, which works great for quick navigation prompts and podcasts — but it lacks the depth needed for listening to music.

If you want fuller sound for music on longer drives, though, I recommend leaning on its Display Only Bluetooth Mode, which lets the screen handle all the CarPlay or Android Auto visuals while your phone routes audio straight to an external Bluetooth speaker.

What makes CarpodGo's lineup such a practical solution for Slate Truck buyers is that you aren't locked into a one-size-fits-all screen. Depending on how much dashboard real estate you want to give up — and how much you want to spend — you can choose between the CarpodGo T4 Plus, the standard CarpodGo T4, or the CarpodGo Mini.

In a recent development, while all three deliver the same 1,000-nit brightness, 60fps wireless CarPlay and Android Auto responsiveness, and magnetic quick-release convenience, they differ mainly in size and price. For example, the CarpodGo T4 offers everything the T4 Plus does, but in a smaller 8.9-inch footprint that won’t crowd the dashboard as much. Meanwhile, I’ve set up the CarpodGo Mini as well and love its smaller 6.9-inch screen, which features a MagSafe-style magnetic mount.

Sources indicate that sure, these are all great options for early adopters of the Slate Truck, but they have practical applications in other vehicles, too. Whether you're trying to modernize an older car that never came with a touchscreen or you bought a newer vehicle that lacks native CarPlay or Android Auto support, CarpodGo offers one of the cleanest, most versatile ways to bring smart connectivity to virtually any cabin.

The CarpodGo Mini features a 6.9-inch, 1,000-nit screen that delivers 60fps wireless CarPlay and Android Auto. What makes it slightly different apart from its size is how it packs a MagSafe-style magnetic mount, easily letting you snap the screen off when you park. And with Dual-Bluetooth Pure Display Mode, it sends audio straight to your car's speakers so sound quality doesn't drop.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it.
  • Recent findings suggest that I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands.
  • Perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it. Here are the three main reasons why the Duo didn’t work out for me, but might for you.

Recent findings suggest that I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands. You can use it one-handed, but for me it’s not nearly as comfortable as the iPhone 18 Pro. It’s too wide and too heavy to be used for long.

Perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions. But that would be a pretty significant shift for me, as there are so many situations when I don’t have both hands free.

Sources indicate that if you already use two hands with your iPhone regularly—perhaps because you have a Pro Max model—then the Duo’s one-handed experience likely won’t bother you. But the more I used the Duo, the more I found myself missing my iPhone 18 Pro.

The biggest value proposition of a foldable is that it’s a 2-in-1 product, letting you have a standard phone but also a tablet-sized display that fits in your pocket.

Industry observers note that I totally get the appeal, and fully expected to love that hybrid design. But after two weeks of trying, I still struggled to find times when I actually wanted to unfold the Duo. And to be clear, that’s a me problem, not an issue with the Duo itself.

Sources indicate that I tried a bunch of apps on the inner display, and struggled to find use cases that—for me—made it worthwhile to open the Duo. But based on the feedback I’ve seen from most Duo owners, I’m very much in the minority.

Recent findings suggest that I know lots of people love the Duo for video, but I don’t watch much video on my iPhone. I almost never watch YouTube, TikTok, or Instagram Reels. And for shows and movies, I stick with my TV screen and an Apple TV 4K.

Sources indicate that multitasking support on iPhone Duo works really well. But when I found myself needing to multitask, I still reached for my iPad Pro with Magic Keyboard attached. A keyboard-free product can’t replace my main computer (nor would I expect it to), and the Duo screen was too small to comfortably work on it.

Last year I bought an iPhone Air and absolutely loved it. Initially, the Air’s less capable camera system didn’t bother me, it was “good enough.”.

It has been revealed that after a few months though, I started missing the Pro camera system more. Then I learned that my wife was pregnant with twins, and I knew I wanted the best possible iPhone cameras to capture their early weeks and months. So I bought an iPhone 18 Pro in September.

In a recent development, I’ve been very impressed by iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera upgrades, and it’s great having a Telephoto lens again too. Since having the best camera system is so crucial for me right now, I knew iPhone Duo couldn’t be my only iPhone.

Industry observers note that I initially planned to dual-carry the two models, using iPhone 18 Pro solely as a camera. But over and over I found myself wishing it was my only iPhone.

I returned mine as well. Beautiful device, but functionally not very good.

Is the iPhone Duo camera good enough for most people? Probably so. But for this year at least, with my twins aging rapidly, it’s not quite right for me. If I loved the Duo for other reasons, I would just use both models. But since I didn’t, I’m happy to stick with the iPhone 18 Pro.

In closing, I want to explicitly state that I don’t think the iPhone Duo is a bad product, and this isn’t a “bad review.”.

The iPhone Duo just isn’t for me. I get the sense, though, that it’s lots of people’s favorite iPhone in years. Apple created its most unique new iPhone model since the original, and there’s plenty to love about it. I’m very curious to see how popular foldables become over time compared to slab models, because each clearly offers pros and cons. But for me, at least right now, the iPhone 18 Pro is my model of choice.

What has your iPhone Duo experience been like so far? Love it? Undecided? Let us know in the comments.

The Vire Clip, a waist-worn wearable that tracks body temperature continuously.

Industry observers note that finnish startup Vire Health has introduced a programme that gives 100 women early access to a wearable that tracks body temperature from the waist. The manufacturer declared Vire 100 at the Slush tech conference in Helsinki on Wednesday.

Participants will buy the first-generation Vire Clip for €449 and help develop it. They will join weekly sessions with women’s health experts and give feedback on how the data could become useful health insights, Vire stated in a statement.

The programme is open to customers in the EU, the UK, Switzerland and Norway, with deliveries starting in December. A wider rollout will follow in 2027.

Most consumer wearables, such as the Oura Ring, take readings from the finger or wrist. The Vire Clip sits at the waist, close to the body’s core, where it tracks temperature continuously.

The manufacturer indicates this lets it track breathing, sleep position and sweating, as well as sleep, movement and heart rate. Vire aims to show women how their temperature changes across the menstrual cycle and in later life stages, such as perimenopause.

“We’ve worked on the technology behind the Vire Clip for more than 10 years,” remarked Antti Immonen, Vire’s chief executive and co-founder.

Immonen’s heat-sensing research began at LUT University, and Vire was founded in 2021 as a spin-off. He built the first clip that year for his newborn daughter, who has a rare condition that affects her breathing during sleep, the company said.

Industry observers note that the device is now used in a sleep study at Helsinki’s Newly introduced Children’s Hospital, according to Vire. It is also part of Our Transitions, a US menopause study led by the nonprofit 4YouandMe, where an optional group is testing whether it can detect hot flashes.

It has been revealed that vire is backed by members of Oura’s founding team, including co-founder Petteri Lahtela. Former Oura chief science officer Hannu Kinnunen is also part of the team.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s almost time to return to Panem as the next chapter of “The Hunger Games,” “Sunrise on the Reaping,” arrives in theaters on Friday (Nov. 20). It’ll tell the story of the 50th annual Hunger Games, known as the Quarter Quell, when a certain Haymitch Abernathy stepped into the arena. As a “Hunger Games” superfan, I can’t wait to watch it. Yes, my tickets are booked!

Industry observers note that if you’re also feeling the hype, you might be looking for a few dystopian movies to keep you fed until “Sunrise on the Reaping." And that’s why I’ve rounded up a trio of worthwhile picks to keep you entertained until you can head to your nearest multiplex. There’s a Japanese thriller that also focuses on a teen deathmatch, a YA adaptation that is actually good (a real rarity), and a Spielberg movie that’s a pop culture-stuffed high-tech adventure.

These dystopian movies will keep your “Hunger Games” hype high until you can watch “Sunrise on the Reaping” in cinemas later this week.

You can’t discuss “The Hunger Games” franchise without somebody popping up to declare “it’s just a ‘Battle Royale’ rip-off.” While I think that argument is pretty asinine, I definitely agree that any fans of “Hunger Games” should check out this 2000 Japanese dystopian action-thriller. It also centers on a group of teens forced to fight to the death, but the Panem pageantry is stripped away. This deathmatch is even more visceral and significantly more violent — “Battle Royale” got an R-rating for very good reason.

According to recent reports, set in a Japan besieged by juvenile delinquency, the government institutes a yearly event called Battle Royale, in which a random high school class is taken to a remote island, each is given a duffle bag containing an assortment of supplies and a random weapon, and then they have three days to kill or be killed. Without the sci-fi trappings of “The Hunger Games,” “Battle Royale” focuses squarely on the horrors of children being forced to fight to the death.

Watch "Battle Royale" on Prime Video now.

In the wake of “The Hunger Games’” success (and “Twilight” before it), Hollywood studios scrambled to adapt any YA novel they could get their hands on. This led to awful films like “Beautiful Creatures,” “The Giver,” and “The Mortal Instruments” (to name just a few). Most didn’t even get one sequel, let alone adapt the whole series, but a rare success story was “The Maze Runner,” which actually completed its franchise run, with a full trilogy.

Based on the novels by James Dashner, “The Maze Runner” movie took the right lessons from “Hunger Games” with a solid young cast, headlined by Dylan O’Brien, and smart direction. It follows a teenage boy named Thomas (O’Brien) who awakens in a vast clearing surrounded by a gigantic stone maze. Along with his fellow teens trapped in the mysterious place, he has to solve the maze to earn his freedom and learn why he was placed there.

Recent findings suggest that the sequels, “The Scorch Trials” and “The Death Cure,” are also pretty good. Though book purists will be disappointed to learn they substantially differ from the novels, stripping away the narrative twists of Dashner’s written work in favor of a more streamlined Hollywood approach.

Watch "The Maze Runner" on Prime Video (buy/rent) now.

Dystopian movies don’t have to be excessively dour. Case in point, Steven Spielberg’s “Ready Player One,” which is full of color, larger-than-life set pieces and endless references to decades gone by, especially the 1980s. In fact, there are probably too many pop culture references, though in fairness to Spielberg, that is also a common criticism of the Ernest Cline novel on which the movie is based. Despite its flaws — it’s a theme park movie, fun in the moment, but also artificial — “Ready Player One” is a breezy watch, and a major midpoint sequence pays homage to one of the best Kubrick flicks ever.

According to recent reports, set in 2045, it’s a grim time for humanity. The population escapes the bleakness of the real world via the Oasis, a virtual reality construct where people can be anything they want. When the Oasis’ creator, James Halliday (Mark Rylance), dies, a posthumous recording kickstarts a hunt through the virtual world for three Easter Eggs; whoever finds the final one will be granted control of the digital universe. Our hero is Wade Watts (Tye Sheridan), who is hoping to find the prize before a sinister corporation.

Watch "Ready Player One" on HBO Max now.
