Industry News: Is the Stock Market Really in an AI Bubble? Wall Street's Doomsayers Are Ignoring Crucial Facts.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (911 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the artificial intelligence (AI) boom began in earnest when OpenAI introduced ChatGPT in November 2022.
  • According to recent reports, however, the enthusiasm has been accompanied by a growing chorus of warnings that AI stocks are in a speculative bubble.
  • Those concerns deserve consideration, and some arguments have merit, but Wall Street's doomsayers seem to be ignoring crucial facts about the stock market's valuation and the economic benefits of AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Trevor Jennewine – Nov 18, 2026 at 5:12AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›.

Sources indicate that the artificial intelligence (AI) boom began in earnest when OpenAI introduced ChatGPT in November 2022. Since then, the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.33%) and Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +0.77%) have advanced 90% and 122%, respectively, as investors have poured money into companies developing AI chips, infrastructure, and software.

According to recent reports, however, the enthusiasm has been accompanied by a growing chorus of warnings that AI stocks are in a speculative bubble. And several prominent financial experts think the boom will end with a devastating stock market crash, potentially dragging the U.S. economy into a recession.

Those concerns deserve consideration, and some arguments have merit, but Wall Street's doomsayers seem to be ignoring crucial facts about the stock market's valuation and the economic benefits of AI.

Image source: OpenAI (AI-generated illustration).

Industry observers note that former SEC Chair Gary Gensler recently warned that artificial intelligence had already formed a stock market bubble that could burst and trigger a recession before the 2028 presidential election. In an interview with CNN, he expressed concern about the massive amount of money being invested in AI infrastructure, particularly the growing reliance on debt and complex financing deals.

In a recent development, admittedly, Gensler makes good points, and he is not alone. Michael Burry, the investor who famously predicted the collapse of the U.S. housing market in 2008, has also warned that technology companies are spending too much relative to profits they are likely to earn. "It is just an asset bubble, plain and simple," he wrote earlier this year. "This, all of it, is the scene of the bloody car crash, minutes before it happens.".

Meanwhile, Jeremy Grantham, co-founder of investment management firm GMO, had this to say in a research paper published earlier this year: "The rule from history is that great technological innovations lead to great bubbles." And investment manager John Hussman believes the S&P 500 could eventually fall between 50% and 75% when the bubble bursts.

In a recent development, these warnings share several common themes. Technology companies are spending an unprecedented amount of money on AI infrastructure, often without a clear timeline for generating returns. Circular financing deals create additional risk, and investors may be overestimating the long-term profitability of AI.

Additionally, many analysts believe stocks are too expensive, and they are quick to point out a particular valuation metric has reached levels last seen during the dot-com bubble.

In a recent development, one metric frequently cited by market bears is the S&P 500's cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (CAPE) ratio, which divides stock prices by average inflation-adjusted earnings over the past decade. The S&P 500's CAPE ratio topped 40 in six consecutive months this year, a level last seen when the dot-com bubble burst in 2000.

However, CAPE is a backward-looking valuation metric. That means it does not account for future earnings growth, which is particularly notable when evaluating a transformative technology like AI. Indeed, forward-looking valuation metrics tell a very different story.

Sources indicate that the S&P 500's forward price-to-earnings (PE) ratio rocketed by 20 and eventually topped 25 as the dot-com bubble built momentum in the late 1990s. That happened because stock prices were appreciating much faster than corporate profits were increasing. The S&P 500's forward PE ratio stayed above 22 until early 2001.

The opposite is happening today. The S&P 500's forward PE ratio topped 23 last year, but the valuation has gradually moderated as earnings growth has accelerated. Today, the S&P 500 trades at 17.7 times forward earnings, according to FactSet Research. That is the cheapest valuation in more than three years, and it's a discount to the 10-year average of 18.9.

Sources indicate that that doesn't sound like a bubble. Of course, that argument depends on companies meeting Wall Street's earnings estimates. But investors have several reasons to believe corporate profits can continue to grow rapidly.

In a recent development, first, AI adoption is happening at an extraordinary pace. The Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis found that generative AI reached 55% of U.S. adults ages 18 to 64 approximately three years after ChatGPT debuted. At comparable stages, personal computers and the internet had adoption rates of just 20% and 30%, respectively.

Second, AI is already generating measurable economic benefits, despite being relatively early in its adoption cycle.

According to recent reports, there are many other examples. Businesses are already using the technology to reduce costs, boost productivity, and create true value. As adoption broadens and applications improve, those benefits could translate into sustained corporate earnings growth.

Of course, none of this means every AI stock is cheap, nor does it guarantee that the stock market will continue rising. Whether a stock is reasonably valued today ultimately depends on how quickly earnings grow tomorrow. But I do not believe there is decisive evidence that AI stocks are in an epic bubble destined to burst with catastrophic consequences. That is certainly possible, but it is not a foregone conclusion.

10 stocks we like better than Vanguard S&P 500 ETF ›.

While the Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF (SCHD -0.64%) is a fraction of VOO's size, with almost $123 billion in AUM, it's the largest ETF focused on dividend stocks.

Both of these top ETFs pay dividends, making them potential options for investors seeking to generate passive income. Here's a look at how much you'd need to invest in each one to generate around $1,000 of dividend income each month.

It has been revealed that the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF tracks the S&P 500 Index, which measures the return of the 500 largest publicly traded U.S. companies. Many of these companies pay dividends, which VOO collects and then distributes to investors each quarter. For example, its top holding is Apple, which currently pays a quarterly dividend of $0.27 per share. However, while many of its holdings pay dividends, the ETF currently has a relatively low yield of around 1%, matching the S&P 500's dividend yield. That's because many of its holdings have lower dividend yields (Apple's is a meager 0.3%).

According to recent reports, at the ETF's current yield of around 1%, you'd need to invest almost $1.2 million into VOO to generate $12,000 in dividend income each year, or around $1,000 per month. That's a hefty investment. On a positive note, the dividend income should grow. The S&P 500 has delivered mid-single-digit annualized dividend growth over the past three years.

NYSEMKT · As of 9:31 AM ET 11/18/26.

Industry observers note that the Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF focuses specifically on dividend-paying stocks. It tracks an index (Dow Jones U.S. Dividend 100 Index) that screens companies based on several dividend-quality characteristics, including yield, five-year dividend growth rate, and financial strength. As a result, the fund holds 100 high-quality, high-yielding dividend growth stocks.

NYSEMKT · As of 9:30 AM ET 11/18/26.

It has been revealed that the ETF currently has a dividend yield of around 3%, based on its payments over the last 12 months. Thanks to its much higher yield, you can generate more income with less capital from SCHD. For example, you'd only need to invest around $400,000 to generate $12,000 of dividend income each year to hit the monthly target of $1,000.

Further, this ETF should deliver faster dividend growth in the future, due to its dual focus on yield and dividend growth. Over the last five years, its average holding has delivered more than 9% annual dividend growth. However, dividend growth has slowed considerably over the past year, with SCHD's payout rising only about 2% over the last 12 months.

Industry observers note that VOO and SCHD both provide investors with passive dividend income. However, thanks to its right now higher yield, you'd need to invest one-third as much capital in SCHD to generate the same amount of dividend income. That makes it the better option for investors seeking to maximize their passive income.

Industry News: ‘We need more reviewers’: Finding Linux bugs is easy now – fixing them is another story

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (765 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recently, Microsoft’s FORGE Lab reported that its AI scanning system, MDASH, turned up 59 upstream Linux kernel bug reports, including one flaw at least 21 years old.
  • Industry observers note that why so many?
  • In the latest Windows Patch Tuesday security release, Microsoft reported 726 CVEs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recently, Microsoft’s FORGE Lab reported that its AI scanning system, MDASH, turned up 59 upstream Linux kernel bug reports, including one flaw at least 21 years old. That’s less impressive than it sounds. For 2026, through Nov. 2, the Linux Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) team reported an average of 27 CVEs a day.

Industry observers note that why so many? Easy: in Linux, any bug can be a security bug. As Linux Torvalds told me in 2024, “Bugs will happen, and anything can be a security bug if somebody is clever enough to just figure out how to abuse it.” Besides, since Linux runs everything from smartphones to refrigerators to supercomputers, what may be a serious bug in one device may not even appear at all on another.

It’s not just Linux, though. In the latest Windows Patch Tuesday security release, Microsoft reported 726 CVEs. The vast majority of these bug reports are coming from AI programmers. Finding bugs on anything is no longer the hard part. But reviewing and fixing them is, and both Microsoft developers and kernel maintainers are struggling to keep up.

Also: Microsoft fixes over 1,000 Windows flaws – and one is being exploited.

As the FORGE Lab remarked, “Finding bugs and fixing them are drastically out of balance.” Turning its findings into reports took more than four person-months because “human effort [is] the bottleneck.”.

That’s hurting the overworked maintainers. On Nov. 10, an ARM engineer and Linux kernel maintainer Lorenzo Stoakes gave up reviewing code. He’d been a reviewer for the memory-management core, misc, reclaim, and Rust-related sections. Stoakes, a kernel contributor since 2014,  wrote, “Given the current throughput in the kernel resulting from AI-generated series, I unfortunately lack the bandwidth to generally be able to offer review except in those areas I maintain.”.

Industry observers note that stoakes added, “Of course the AI wave has been horrible, and is getting significantly worse. At first it was once in a while that I’d see slop. Then it was at least once a week. Then every few days. Nowadays it’s pretty much half of what I see, if not more.”.

Also: Filing bugs for open-source apps is a huge help for devs – and easier than you think.

He’s not alone. As Greg Kroah-Hartman, the Linux kernel stable maintainer, said in a Q&A session at Open Source Summit Europe, “We don’t have enough people to review them, the onslaught of the LLM-generated patches. We need more reviewers. We don’t have enough. All of the maintainers are burnt out, and we have been for ten years.”.

It’s not all doom and gloom, though. Linux Torvalds, Linux’s creator, mentioned in a recent Linux Kernel Mailing List (LKML) message that much of the new code in the Linux 7.4 rc 2 “was driven by various AI fixes.”.

He continued, “that on the bpf [Berkeley Packet Filter]- side at least the fixes are now coming in faster than the upcoming reports, and that sounds lovely if true. I think most other areas haven’t reached that point yet, but it’s at least a sign that we _may_ be starting to see the tide starting to turn. Don’t hold your breath, but maybe cross your fingers we’ll be getting there in the not entirely distant future.”.

Recent findings suggest that we can but hope. In an interview, Kroah-Hartman isn’t so optimistic. “We are getting closer, yes, but not quite there yet.”  He’s not even willing to give a guesstimate of when human-approved AI fixes will catch up with and overcome AI bug reports.

Also: I locked down my OpenClaw agent with Claude Code – then dared it to escape.

Daniel Steinberg, the creator of the open-source cURL project, is also cautiously optimistic. Steinberg, who’s been especially critical of AI slop bug reports, told me in an interview that he now believes “we manage the flood pretty well so far, even if it goes a little up and down in periods depending exactly on who sends us a new set of findings this particular week.”.

Still, while AI bugs remain a major headache for now, AI bug fixes, along with the work of thousands of maintainers, may finally be starting to stem the AI bug flood. I still foresee long days and nights of work ahead.

Recent findings suggest that I also expect we’ll see more serious security breaches. In November alone, we saw a serious Linux TCP networking security hole revealed; the nasty Alpine Linux OpenSSH flaw; Alpine’s GitLab near-miss; and the wide-open PHP2Shell security problem, which many groups still haven’t patched.

I checked Gemini’s fresh Memory summary to see what it knew about me – how to see and edit yours

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (661 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that like any AI, Google Gemini wants to remember things about you.
  • Also: I tried Claude Sheets on 3 tasks – and it saved me hours of work.
  • With a upcoming option called Memory summary, you’re able to view the details that Gemini has gathered about you over time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that like any AI, Google Gemini wants to remember things about you. The purported reason is to help tailor and personalize your conversations. But remember that your personal details may also wind up training the AI or even being reviewed by actual humans. With that in mind, you might want to find out just what Gemini knows about you. And now you can.

Also: I tried Claude Sheets on 3 tasks – and it saved me hours of work.

With a upcoming option called Memory summary, you’re able to view the details that Gemini has gathered about you over time. These may be tidbits from your conversations or things that you directly told the AI. Even better, you can add or remove any details just by editing the memory or issuing your request directly to Gemini.

This fresh capability is available in Gemini across the board, so you can access it at the Gemini website, in the mobile iOS and Android apps, and in the Windows and Mac desktop apps.

Sources indicate that launch Gemini via the web or in one of the mobile or desktop apps. In the left pane displaying your previous chats, select the Settings icon at the bottom. At the Settings screen, select Personal Intelligence and then click or tap Memory summary. If the option is grayed out, it means the Memory feature is turned off. To proceed, turn it back on. You can always turn if off again afterward if you wish.

You’ll then see the individual details by category. My summary arranged the information across such categories as Essentials, Business & Career, Reading & Interests, and Culinary Preferences. Go down the list to see the individual items in each category. To view a recent history, tap the three dot-icon at the top and select Memory history. This highlights you the latest changes and updates to Gemini’s memory.

Also: Stop sharing your passwords with AI agents.

What if Gemini’s memory includes details that are too personal or just incorrect? No problem. You can alter the AI’s memories of you. At the website or in one of the desktop apps, click the pencil icon at the top. Now you’re able to directly edit the text to add, remove, or revise specific details. After you’ve made your changes, just click Save.

It has been revealed that for example, my summary stated that I lived in Madison County. I have no idea where Gemini got that notion, as I live in Newly introduced York. Here, I revised the text and saved the changes, which then synced across the Gemini website and apps.

The mobile apps have no direct editing capability. But there’s another method that works both on mobile and on the desktop. Just tell Gemini what change you want to make. At the prompt, type and speak your request, and the AI will carry it out for you.

Also: The best and worst AI for your privacy, ranked.

In a recent development, as an example, my summary remarked that I run a business called Batter Up selling collectible baseball cards. That’s not at all true. I had once referred to such a store only to test Gemini’s image creation skills to design a logo for a baseball card seller. Here, I simply told Gemini that I don’t run a business called Batter Up and asked it to remove that item from its memory. Poof, that detail promptly disappeared.

Industry observers note that google isn’t exactly known as being privacy-friendly, and that extends to Gemini. In this case, though, I give the tech giant credit for offering this easy way to control the AI’s memories. I do find the memory feature useful as it recalls details about me that help personalize and direct its responses. But I don’t like Gemini or Google knowing too much about me. Now I can keep memory enabled and just control what it remembers about me.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • 10 stocks we like better than Circle Internet Group ›.
  • The ongoing cryptocurrency bear market is exposing fundamental differences between businesses operating in the digital asset economy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By RJ Fulton – Updated Nov 18, 2026 at 5:25AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Circle Internet Group ›.

The ongoing cryptocurrency bear market is exposing fundamental differences between businesses operating in the digital asset economy. Circle Internet Group (CRCL +1.08%) and Strategy (MSTR -6.34%) offer investors two distinct ways to gain exposure to the industry, but their financial performance depends on very different factors.

Industry observers note that circle is building the financial infrastructure behind digital payments through its USDC (USDC -0.01%) stablecoin, generating revenue primarily from interest earned on its reserves. Strategy, meanwhile, has transformed itself from an enterprise software manufacturer into a Bitcoin (BTC -3.10%) treasury business, leveraging capital markets to accumulate increasingly large holdings of the cryptocurrency.

While both companies stand to benefit from the long-term adoption of digital assets, their contrasting business models, capital structures, and exposure to cryptocurrency volatility could have significant implications for shareholder returns heading into 2027.

With services spanning 185 countries, Circle is positioned to benefit from the growing integration of blockchain technology into traditional finance. Unlike many cryptocurrency businesses, Circle does not depend directly on rising digital asset prices to drive revenue. Instead, it earns the majority of its revenue from interest generated on USDC reserves.

Recent findings suggest that in the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $3 billion, representing year-over-year growth of approximately 25.7%. Net income totaled $462.9 million, translating to a profit margin of roughly 15.4%. The expanding use of stablecoins for payments and financial settlement provides Circle with a structural growth opportunity that extends beyond speculative cryptocurrency trading.

Sources indicate that as of December 2025, Circle maintained a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.0 and a current ratio of 1.0. The company generated approximately $529.7 million in free cash flow during fiscal 2025. However, stock-based compensation represented 104.4% of operating cash flow, warranting closer scrutiny of the quality of its cash generation.

Although Strategy continues to operate its enterprise analytics software business, its investment thesis increasingly centers on accumulating Bitcoin. The tech giant utilizes a combination of common stock, preferred securities, and debt financing to expand its Bitcoin holdings, providing shareholders with exposure to the cryptocurrency through a traditional equity structure.

According to recent reports, over the latest 12-month reporting period, revenue reached approximately $495.1 million, representing year-over-year growth of 4.2%. However, Strategy reported a net loss of approximately $13.7 billion, primarily reflecting declines in the fair value of its Bitcoin holdings. The disparity between revenue and net income illustrates how much Bitcoin's price movements now overshadow the financial performance of its software business.

As of December 2025, Strategy maintained a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.2 and a current ratio of 5.6. Despite these seemingly favorable balance sheet metrics, the organization recorded negative free cash flow of $112.5 million in fiscal 2025. With limited internal cash generation, Strategy remains heavily dependent on external financing to support its Bitcoin accumulation strategy.

Recent findings suggest that one of Circle's primary risks is intensifying competition. Efforts to formalize stablecoin regulation, most notably through the GENIUS Act, lend legitimacy to the industry but also open the door for banks, payment processors, and fintech companies to glitch competing stablecoins, potentially eroding Circle's market share and profitability. Circle is also sensitive to interest rates, as falling short-term Treasury yields could reduce reserve income unless offset by growth in USDC circulation.

It has been revealed that strategy faces a different set of risks. The company frequently issues upcoming shares to fund Bitcoin purchases, which can dilute the ownership of existing shareholders. While selling new shares has historically worked in Strategy's favor during bull markets, a prolonged bear market makes this approach less effective. As Bitcoin's price declines, Strategy risks having to problem additional shares to fund further purchases, potentially diluting existing shareholders without delivering a corresponding increase in per-share value.

While Circle appears more reasonably valued based on its P/S ratio, Strategy currently offers a lower multiple relative to its future earnings estimates.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

Investors should note that the Forward P/E compares the current stock price to future earnings estimates. The P/S ratio measures the tech giant market cap against sales over the past twelve months.

Despite Circle's relatively expensive forward price-to-earnings ratio of 53.2 compared to Strategy's 6.5, I believe Circle offers the more compelling investment opportunity heading into 2027. Strategy's seemingly attractive earnings multiple warrants caution, as its profitability is heavily influenced by fluctuations in Bitcoin's price rather than the underlying performance of its software business. Circle also trades at just 5.4 times sales, compared to Strategy's 93.1, although traditional valuation metrics are less useful when evaluating a Bitcoin treasury company.

Ultimately, the deciding factor for me is the sustainability of each company's business model. Stablecoins represent one of the most practical applications of blockchain technology, with opportunities extending across cross-border payments, commercial transactions, and institutional financial settlement. Circle can capitalize on this growing adoption regardless of whether Bitcoin enters another bull market.

Sources indicate that strategy could deliver substantial returns if Bitcoin rebounds in 2027. However, its dependence on capital markets and potential shareholder dilution introduce additional risks that investors would not encounter by simply owning Bitcoin. While Circle faces competitive pressures and a demanding earnings valuation of its own, I prefer its ability to generate revenue from the broader adoption of digital assets rather than relying on their price appreciation.

Starting this week, customers booking an Uber ride in Las Vegas could be matched with a Zoox autonomous vehicle.

Industry observers note that zoox’s boxy, purpose-built vehicles have been operating for the general public in Sin City for a little over a year via the tech giant’s own app. But this is the first time Zoox, which is owned by Amazon, is teaming up with a third-party platform like Uber. (You can still hail a ride in Vegas through the Zoox app; the company began charging passengers in August.).

In a recent development, now, riders who request an UberX, Uber Comfort, Uber Electric, Uber Comfort Electric or Wait & Save could be paired with a Zoox robotaxi, and they won’t have to pay extra. You can boost your chances of being matched with the AV by going to Ride Preferences in the Uber app’s settings. Then tap Autonomous vehicles, and hit the toggle next to Get more autonomous rides.

After you’ve been matched with a Zoox vehicle, you can choose to accept the autonomous ride or opt for a non-AV. Passengers can access 24/7 human support from both the Uber app and inside the Zoox vehicle.

Unlike other autonomous vehicles from companies like Waymo and Wayve, which retrofit cars from third-party manufacturers, Zoox’s purpose-built robotaxis don’t have a steering wheel, driver’s seat or pedals. Instead, there are two rows of seats facing each other, so you can chat more easily with your fellow passengers. The vehicles are bidirectional, making it a little easier to get out of a parking space, for instance. I’ve taken a few Zoox rides in Las Vegas and San Francisco, and despite the robotaxi’s unique design, the experience felt remarkably ordinary, with the vehicle seamlessly navigating through traffic.

It has been revealed that uber and Zoox confirmed their multiyear partnership in March. The companies also strategy to hit the road together in Los Angeles in 2027, after Zoox releases there via its own app.

In a recent development, teaming up with Uber could expose Zoox to more customers, since many people already have the ride-hailing app downloaded on their phones. A tourist hub like Las Vegas has become a hotspot for AV companies to test and launch their services, with many people willing to try something fresh as they get around the city.

“Zoox has built something truly unique, and by bringing its purpose-built robotaxis to Uber, we’re introducing an entirely new riding experience to more people in Las Vegas, with Los Angeles coming next,” Samarth Kejriwal, global head of autonomous mobility at Uber, said in a statement.

Industry observers note that this comes after the dissolution of Uber’s exclusive partnership with Alphabet-owned Waymo in Austin and Atlanta, which Bloomberg reports will end starting early next year. Instead, Waymo reportedly intends to offer rides directly within its own app, as it does in several other locations. Meanwhile, Uber has partnered with dozens of other AV companies, including Aurora, Wayve, Avride, Nuro and May Mobility.

Recent findings suggest that while Waymo is the leader in the self-driving space, Zoox has been ramping up its operations in recent months. Along with Las Vegas, riders can join a waitlist to ride in San Francisco, with plans to roll out its robotaxi service in Miami and Austin. Zoox is also testing its self-driving technology in Seattle, Atlanta, Los Angeles, Dallas, Phoenix, Houston, San Diego and Washington, DC.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the best AI models on the market couldn’t find zero-days earlier this year, but now they can in less than 15 minutes and at a cost of a few bucks, according to a latest report from penetration testing firm Xint.io.
  • Every major AI developer is working at breakneck speed to improve model effectiveness.
  • This is good news for businesses trying to harness AI for productivity and newly introduced services, but as token prices fall, it has also become cheaper for attackers to launch AI-assisted attacks, including software breaches caused by exploiting unknown vulnerabilities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the best AI models on the market couldn’t find zero-days earlier this year, but now they can in less than 15 minutes and at a cost of a few bucks, according to a latest report from penetration testing firm Xint.io. The findings raise questions about how vulnerabilities will be discovered and exploited in the future.

Every major AI developer is working at breakneck speed to improve model effectiveness. At the same time, token prices continue to fall, with studies showing that the average cost of tokens, which varies by domain, has dropped by about 47% per quarter since 2023 and 15% last month alone, due to intense competition among companies including OpenAI and Anthropic.

This is good news for businesses trying to harness AI for productivity and newly introduced services, but as token prices fall, it has also become cheaper for attackers to launch AI-assisted attacks, including software breaches caused by exploiting unknown vulnerabilities.

Also: How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain.

Sources indicate that A report published by Xint.io examines how popular AI models have evolved over the past year to the point where cybersecurity tasks that would have failed only months ago now succeed. The team analyzed seven models rolled out since February 2026: two from OpenAI, three from Anthropic, and two open-source models from DeepSeek and Z.ai. The team tracked, over time, how they performed in finding a target vulnerability.

It has been revealed that the target of this research was a security flaw in Google’s V8 engine. Tracked as CVE-2026-102321, the type confusion bug leading to remote code execution (RCE) was disclosed to the Google Vulnerability Reward Program (VRP) by Xint researcher Taisic Yun and so was not present in the AI models’ training datasets.

The research scope was limited to a set of source files, including the file containing the vulnerability, and each model was instructed to search for security issues within these files.

Sources indicate that xint’s first test was conducted in February. After 25 hours and $350 of scanning, the best models then available still couldn’t find the critical vulnerability.

In July, GPT 5.6 Sol found the zero-day flaw for $22 in 44 minutes.

Also: Finding Linux bugs is easy – fixing them is another story.

By September, GPT 6 Sol discovered the bug in 13 minutes for only $4.24 with its first guided prompt.

Only three of the seven models found the bug: GPT 6 Sol, GPT 5.6 Sol, and Claude Opus 5, all launched from July onward. GPT 5.6 Sol needed two prompts, while Claude Opus 5 found it on its first try but at a higher cost of $43.40.

DeepSeek’s and Z.ai’s models failed the task.

The researchers say that the combination of AI model development and low token prices means that “mediocre hackers” can now use frontier models effectively to discover and potentially exploit vulnerabilities, and “while we are still far from complete amateurs using unharnessed models to hack systems and applications, what used to be considered too hard and costly to be worth the effort of the average hacker is now reachable.”.

As a result, organizations need to adjust their security posture accordingly — but falling token costs and evolving AI skills and speed can also work in your favor.

Also: How I safely run my OpenClaw AI agent 24/7 on a Mac.

It has been revealed that there’s nothing stopping an organization’s security team or pentesters from running the same checks themselves to find vulnerabilities before threat actors do. AI-assisted tests, arguably, are no longer something that can be pushed back to next year’s budgetary review. By performing a risk assessment that focuses on likely weak spots, such as public-facing services or a digital supply chain that hasn’t been audited for years, organizations can mitigate the risk AI-enabled cyberattacks pose.

Recent findings suggest that zero-day vulnerabilities are unknown to vendors, and a patch might not be available when they go public or are actively exploited in the wild. So, AI can only go so far, but it can free up your defenders for tasks that need the human touch. Furthermore, maintaining zero-trust access controls, segmenting and shoring up your network’s defenses, and monitoring endpoints for signs of suspicious behavior can do as much as, or more than, AI.

As Xint notes, “expertise still matters” when it comes to instructing AI models to discover vulnerabilities. In some cases, the models couldn’t find the target vulnerability without guidance, so additional runs were needed, increasing time and cost.

“Software breaches still require some level of technical proficiency,” the researchers say, “but no longer top-of-the-distribution expertise.”.

Breaking: Did a Single Router Ground the Nation’s Flights? Experts Express Doubt

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1040 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The humble internet router is at the center of another national firestorm.
  • Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said Sunday that a single router in Arkansas was to blame for the nearly 5-hour-long ground stop on Friday.
  • FAA investigators zeroed in on a routine network upgrade at a radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, where a copper wire line was being upgraded to fiber optic cable by the contractor L3Harris.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The humble internet router is at the center of another national firestorm.

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said Sunday that a single router in Arkansas was to blame for the nearly 5-hour-long ground stop on Friday. It was only the second nationwide halt to US air travel since Sept. 11, 2001, leading to the cancellation of 12,462 flights on Friday alone.

FAA investigators zeroed in on a routine network upgrade at a radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, where a copper wire line was being upgraded to fiber optic cable by the contractor L3Harris. A new router that came online during the upgrade may have overwhelmed the older equipment, investigators say.

“Either through contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment, that router that was being replaced as we switched from copper to fiber, it started flooding other routers in our air traffic control system,” Duffy said in an interview Sunday.

This sent a barrage of data through the FAA’s internal communication system — about 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds – that air traffic controllers use to help guide pilots through the country’s airspace. When that fresh router was turned on, agency officials noticed the same problems at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, which had undergone similar work weeks before, Duffy remarked. The routers at the Arkansas and Texas facilities led to 17 out of the FAA’s 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers experiencing network instability, according to the agency.

But some aviation experts say this official explanation strains credulity.

“I don’t think it’s plausible,” Robert W. Mann Jr., the founder of airline analysis and consulting firm R.W. Mann & Company, told CNET. “Given the network architecture, which is fully duplicative and has fallback capabilities on every link and every piece of physical hardware, it’s not credible that one or even two routers would be an problem.”.

It has been revealed that the impacts of the nationwide ground stop are reverberating on the other side of the weekend. As of 3:30 p.m. EST, 333 flights within, into or out of the US have been canceled Monday, according to flight tracking website FlightAware, and more than 3,800 have been delayed.

The FAA router that grounded tens of thousands of flights looks a lot different from the one that sits in your home. These industrial-grade devices, called switches, are much larger than home Wi-Fi routers and built to withstand harsh conditions. While the agency pointed to the single router in Arkansas as the cause of Friday’s complications, it claims it disabled 60 similar units as a precaution.

In a recent development, FAA Administrator Brian Bedford said Saturday that the agency is in the process of replacing around 2,000 Cisco routers with 600 Juniper routers. Could any one of those routine equipment upgrades suddenly overload the FAA’s communications system?

In a recent development, “What surprised me most is the redundancy part for this type of national infrastructure,” Ilia Rabinovich, vice president at the cybersecurity firm Sygnia, told CNET. “This is one of the first things we discuss with clients in terms of preparedness – having backups, having redundancy connectivity, having different connections that you can migrate to different places.”.

Mann thought the timing and symptoms pointed to a new $875 million AI-supported air traffic management tool called Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories, or SMART.

“What they did starting in September at Baltimore-Washington is at a very low level, for about 60 days. It had managed about 180 flights in total over 60 days,” Mann said. “And then suddenly in November, they revealed they would implement that system across all 22 continental US air traffic control centers.”.

“You went from subscale to superscale based upon 60 days of very, very limited testing, and within two days, you had the meltdown that they should have known was likely to occur,” Mann noted.

According to recent reports, on Oct. 13, more than 25 lawmakers sent a letter to the FAA asking it to pause the rollout of the tool, citing a lack of transparency and training for air traffic controllers.

“We have heard from several sources that frontline aviation safety workers were notified of the SMART tool rollout mere days in advance or not at all, giving them no time to learn how the system works, how it is incorporated into their workflow, and what oversight and accountability mechanisms maintain aviation safety standards,” the letter indicates.

Sources indicate that the FAA says in an FAQ page on the incident that the SMART system wasn’t responsible for the matter. A representative for the agency didn’t immediately respond to CNET’s request for comment.

The FAA’s acting CTO, Rebecca Guy, said at a press conference Saturday that the FAA identified the routers in Arkansas and Texas and disabled “both of those right away and were able to stabilize our network.” But the Transportation Secretary’s interviews over the weekend didn’t instill a lot of confidence in the FAA network’s resilience.

“We have old switches, old routers. We use 1980s little copper lines. It’s an old system that went down and went down everywhere. It got overloaded,” Duffy said at a Friday night news conference.

Industry observers note that the FAA has upgraded over 3,500 of its communication lines to fiber, but more than 5,000 copper lines are still scheduled to be replaced by the end of 2028. It’s eye-opening to see how reliant the FAA still is on copper lines, a technology that the Federal Communications Commission has for years deemed insufficient for average home internet users.

It didn’t take long for officials to point to funding as the ultimate cause of Friday’s groundings. Duffy repeatedly called for more funding over the weekend in order to upgrade the outdated system.

“The government and FAA are looked on as the piñata here because every time you beat on FAA or beat on the government for not doing a good job, money falls out,” Mann said. “It didn’t take, what, 6 hours, before we had a cabinet secretary basically saying if we gave him $50 billion, he would fix all this.”.

Duffy had asked for $30 billion for the FAA in September. After Friday’s fiasco, he increased his request by $20 billion.

By Marc Guberti – Nov 18, 2026 at 5:30AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Nebius Group ›.

Industry observers note that nebius Group (NBIS +2.90%) stock lost 17% of its value after delivering earnings on Nov. 12, which looks like a good buying opportunity. Broader artificial intelligence headwinds have been dragging down the entire AI trade, with Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia acting as one of the latest gut punches.

Recent findings suggest that the bad earnings reaction does not change the long-term fundamentals, which have continued to strengthen. While Nebius may have negative short-term sentiment, the future continues to look bright, warranting a closer look at current levels.

Sources indicate that naturally, the earnings report wasn't perfect. There were some real issues, but they are short-term problems that the tech giant will solve. For instance, some of the capacity from the $17.4 billion, five-year Microsoft (MSFT +0.00%) infrastructure deal was delayed to Q2 2027. Previously, all of that capacity was supposed to be available by the end of the year.

It's not a problem with Nebius' execution. That's a good thing and a bad thing. The good thing is that when Nebius builds its own data centers, it's usually on time. However, the bad news is that some of Nebius' revenue is tied to colocation sites. In other words, Nebius does not own the facilities for those data centers.

Colocation introduces more execution risks and also increases expenses in the future. Nebius doesn't own the entire stack for all of its AI build-outs in the same way that Iren (IREN +1.55%) does. The company hinted at that in the Q3 shareholder letter, saying that future gigawatts will come from sites it owns while citing third-party delays as a major reason for the shift.

NASDAQ · As of 9:30 AM ET 11/18/26.

In its Q2 results, Nebius guided for $7 billion to $9 billion in annual recurring revenue (ARR) by the end of the year. The company pushed that target to $7 billion-plus by February and believes it will be in that range before the Latest Jersey site tied to the Microsoft deal is at full capacity.

This delay caused some concerns and is part of the reason why the stock dropped by 17% on earnings. However, does a delay for this lofty ARR target from December 2026 to February 2027 really mean anything if you zoom out five years?

It's a small snag in timing that does not change the thesis. Furthermore, the delay is due to a colocation facility, and Nebius is increasingly moving away from that model for future AI data centers. The problems are small rather than structural, which makes the current price drop a good buying opportunity.

Some investors were worried about Nebius projecting $40 billion to $45 billion in capital expenditures in 2027, but that's the nature of building large data centers that require AI chips. Some of the best parts of the business model suggest that Nebius can comfortably cover its capital expenditure requirements.

For instance, customer prepayments now cover all of its capital expenditures tied to Q3 agreements. These expenditures include GPUs, data center construction, and leasehold improvement costs, according to Nebius' Q3 shareholder letter. In 2027, 75% to 85% of Nebius' capital expenditures are expected to be covered by prepayments and available investment-grade asset-backed financing.

Industry observers note that nebius' cash balance, credit facilities, and revenue surge may be enough to cover the gap. Its megawatt values continue to climb, with Q3 deals averaging more than $25 million per megawatt, compared to a range of $20 million to $25 million per megawatt in the second quarter.

According to recent reports, rising megawatt values have also reduced the payback period of future deals from 1 year and 10 months to 1 year and 7 months. Trimming the payback period by three months in a single quarter highlights Nebius' strong traction, and this payback window excludes prepayments.

Sources indicate that nebius is targeting $12 billion to $13 billion in revenue next year. It implies that revenue will quadruple from current levels, and if that growth continues, this dip can be a generational buying opportunity.

Your enterprise AI access can be sold for pennies – beware ‘LLM Mixers’

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (853 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in just a few years, businesses have adopted AI and large language models (LLMs) to manage everything from calendar invites to data analysis and programming.
  • Google’s latest report on AI threats, the Q4 AI Threat Tracker from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), found that gateways called LLM Mixers are selling access for cents on the dollar.
  • Also: 6 essential strategies to defend against AI-powered threat actors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in just a few years, businesses have adopted AI and large language models (LLMs) to manage everything from calendar invites to data analysis and programming. Bad actors steal credentials for those models through LLMjacking — and the marketplace is evolving.

Google’s latest report on AI threats, the Q4 AI Threat Tracker from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), found that gateways called LLM Mixers are selling access for cents on the dollar.

Also: 6 essential strategies to defend against AI-powered threat actors.

In a recent development, organizations have poured billions of dollars into AI development and deployment, although the amount they spend on AI tokens every month varies. According to Ramp AI index data, among firms paying for AI, the top 1% spent over $10,000 per employee per month, compared with around $16 for the median firm. When employees have access to AI models, companies may introduce spending caps, but smaller outfits may overlook them.

Industry observers note that LLMjacking is the theft of AI-related credentials, including usernames and passwords, or API keys, used to access AI models. This gives cybercriminals the opportunity to use tokens and AI resources belonging to a victim organization (or individual), typically with usage-based billing or subscriptions with no fixed cap.

With these credentials, an unauthorized user could run high-resource computing tasks, manage their own malicious AI deployments, extract and steal corporate data from the AI’s memory, or even poison training data. To add insult to injury, if demand outstrips the limits of the victim’s subscription, cybercriminals can rack up high usage costs that the victim is then on the hook for.

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

John Hultquist, chief analyst for GTIG, previously noted the cybersecurity unit has seen a “major increase” in LLMjacking over 2026, so we can assume this trend will likely continue into 2027 and beyond.

AI access is now a lucrative illegal business in its own right, leading to what Google calls LLM Mixers: “illicit storefronts” that provide unauthorized access to AI services and underlying proxy infrastructure.

After analyzing LLMJacking vendor advertisements on Russian- and Chinese-language marketplaces, GTIG researchers found that most offer access not only to frontier models from AI labs, but also to jailbroken models marketed as suitable for malicious purposes.

However, it doesn’t seem that many of these cybercriminal groups can agree on “reasonable” pricing, with prices swinging wildly depending on the models offered and the credentials available.

Also: How I safely run my OpenClaw AI agent 24/7 on a Mac – with Claude Code standing guard.

Free trial credentials fetch far less than enterprise credentials, as you would expect. Token prices for business use ranged from $0.10 to $25, and one vendor, APIMart, increased its token price fivefold once a prompt exceeds 100,000 tokens. Other vendors offer subscription-based pricing.

It has been revealed that this might not seem like much at the lower tiers, but Sysdig estimates LLMJacking could cost around $46,000 based on earlier models, and even over $100,000 per day on cutting-edge models. Mandiant research published earlier this month recorded incidents with illicit AI usage exceeding $100,000 in only 24 hours, with cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1 million before access was revoked.

While direct credentials can be sold, the infrastructure element is also an interesting service offering. Google’s threat team noted in the report that the sale of LLM infrastructure “routes buyer traffic through a pool of stolen credentials and compute instances to ensure reliable access, while also offering the ability to spread query volume across multiple victim environments to reduce the likelihood of detection.”.

It has been revealed that LLM Mixers look similar to the rest of the cybercriminal underground economy, in which traders tend to specialize in one or two parts of an attack chain. For example, an LLM Mixer offers the access and infrastructure needed to exploit an enterprise AI model, while its partners might break into victim networks to secure initial access or buy stolen credentials from operators of infostealer malware.

Avoid LLMjacking and having your organization’s AI added to a Mixer’s menu similarly to how you would prevent intrusions into SaaS applications and cloud setups: managing access, monitoring, and imposing restrictions.

Sources indicate that usage and spending are the first areas to tackle. By setting limits on how many tokens can be issued and used across every AI service and account, and by alerting when usage suddenly spikes, organizations can limit damage if an account is compromised and stop massive bills before they rack up.

Also: Can you still trust Proton?

It has been revealed that organizations should also try to prevent their keys from ending up in the hands of cyberattackers in the first place. Google recommends using a secrets manager that securely stores and frequently rotates API keys, and running audits to detect quiet probing, misconfigurations, or shadow accounts.

It’s also advisable, across the board, to implement phishing protections and multi-factor authentication (MFA) to make the business of stealing credentials or compromising your accounts and networks more difficult in the first place.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the last year, a backlash against surveillance technologies from companies like Flock Safety has caused agencies in communities, including Los Angeles and Dayton, Ohio, to reevaluate or cancel their contracts for tools such as license plate reader cameras and drones.
  • Now, some college and high school campuses are taking the same steps, reconsidering whether the value of identifying potential crime suspects or providing first-responder information is worth the privacy trade-offs.
  • A recent story in The Guardian points to dozens of schools, mostly college campuses, where contracts with Flock have been discontinued or where student protests and activism are pressuring administrations to cut ties.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the last year, a backlash against surveillance technologies from companies like Flock Safety has caused agencies in communities, including Los Angeles and Dayton, Ohio, to reevaluate or cancel their contracts for tools such as license plate reader cameras and drones.

Now, some college and high school campuses are taking the same steps, reconsidering whether the value of identifying potential crime suspects or providing first-responder information is worth the privacy trade-offs.

A recent story in The Guardian points to dozens of schools, mostly college campuses, where contracts with Flock have been discontinued or where student protests and activism are pressuring administrations to cut ties. Some of the schools that have walked away from Flock include Cornell University, Emory University, Penn State University and Stanford University, where a coalition called Safe Stanford successfully organized to convince school officials. At Stanford, the university chose to switch from Flock to technology from Genetec, which stores data for only an hour and doesn’t share information with third parties.

Some of the most recent campus protests against using Flock technology have been on the University of Iowa campus, where 2,000 petition signatures were delivered to campus police, and at the University of Kentucky, where student groups chanted, “Flock out! Flock off!”.

Flock, which is one of several companies, including Axon Enterprise, Motorola Solutions and Palantir Technologies, that provide surveillance hardware and software to law enforcement, has been heavily criticized for license plate reader failure rates and abuses within law enforcement.

In an email to CNET, the Atlanta-based company declined to offer the number of colleges or schools it works with, though a recent research paper published in Policing & Society put the number at around 150.

Flock stressed in its email to CNET that customers it contracts with own and control their own data.

“Students deserve to feel safe at school, and Flock license plate reader technology has a measurable impact on helping to solve crimes and increase public safety,” the spokesperson said. “Flock LPR cameras capture a point-in-time image of the rear of a vehicle. Flock does not use facial recognition, cannot identify who is inside a vehicle and cannot determine who the vehicle is registered to.”.

When government agencies like police departments or county sheriff’s offices employ a manufacturer like Flock to provide surveillance services, it typically involves installing cameras in public locations and pointing them at street intersections or on buildings.

According to recent reports, college and high school campuses may have different rules for on-campus surveillance and for public schools. They might also be bound by state laws that also apply to government agencies.

“Campuses also raise concerns ordinary public streets don’t: students often live there, many are minors, and student-privacy laws and school-search rules vary by state, as do limits on how long plate data can be kept and shared,” said Amy Peikoff, an attorney for the Pacific Legal Foundation.

Peikoff mentioned that most courts have allowed the collection of the types of data Flock Safety collects. However, Peikoff said that problems can arise regarding how long agencies such as police departments or schools can retain the data they collect. In the past, activists have pointed to abuses that have occurred when law enforcement workers inappropriately accessed or shared information collected by Flock, in some cases, using it for stalking.

“Maintaining a vast, queryable database of location histories of individuals about whom there’s no particularized suspicion not only presents an opportunity for abuse, but is in itself, I believe, a Fourth Amendment violation,” Peikoff stated.

Lost or stolen Windows laptop? IT can lock it down without wiping it now

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft is testing a newly introduced feature that lets IT admins instantly lock down your lost or stolen device via remote connection, protecting your work projects and personal data from theft and unauthorized access.
  • Also: Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now.
  • The newly introduced remote lock feature is designed to work in tandem with other Microsoft services, such as Intune and BitLocker, to manage a fleet of devices both in-office and remotely across the globe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft is testing a newly introduced feature that lets IT admins instantly lock down your lost or stolen device via remote connection, protecting your work projects and personal data from theft and unauthorized access.

Also: Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now.

The newly introduced remote lock feature is designed to work in tandem with other Microsoft services, such as Intune and BitLocker, to manage a fleet of devices both in-office and remotely across the globe.

Industry observers note that once a device is reported missing or stolen, an admin can disable login access from anywhere without having to fully wipe the laptop or smartphone. Microsoft reports that the lockdown will persist across restarts, even if the device is disconnected from Wi-Fi networks, and can only be lifted by an admin. This means that thieves can’t use your passwords, PINs, or biometric data to circumvent the lock.

In a recent development, while the upcoming feature allows IT admins to respond quickly when a laptop or phone is reported missing, there are still security gaps that other Windows controls must address. The new lock feature doesn’t erase your data or wipe your device if it can’t be recovered, nor does it isolate the missing device from corporate networks. Therefore, IT admins will still need to access those controls via the Intune and Microsoft Entra dashboards.

Also: You can now restore Windows 11 even if it can’t boot up.

The remote lock feature also doesn’t change your Microsoft account credentials, so you can use your log-ins on other devices to recover your data, change passwords, and temporarily disable permissions. Finally, Remote lock doesn’t block the device from being booted in Safe Mode, from a USB, in Windows Recovery Mode, or if the storage drive is reimaged; Microsoft highly recommends keeping BitLocker enabled until the device can be wiped or recovered.

Latest Update: CNET Survey: $75 Billion in Holiday Packages Could Be Vulnerable to Lurking Porch Pirates

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Imagine patiently waiting for the special-edition Legend of Zelda Nintendo Switch 2 console or the upcoming iPhone Duo to be delivered to your door — only for it to disappear seconds after arrival.
  • Sources indicate that online holiday shopping has become the go-to way for many US adults to conveniently find, compare and buy must-have gifts.
  • Sources indicate that CNET’s annual package theft survey polls US adults about their experiences with porch pirates and how they try to prevent it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Imagine patiently waiting for the special-edition Legend of Zelda Nintendo Switch 2 console or the upcoming iPhone Duo to be delivered to your door — only for it to disappear seconds after arrival. That’s the risky reality we’re facing this holiday season because of porch pirates.

Sources indicate that online holiday shopping has become the go-to way for many US adults to conveniently find, compare and buy must-have gifts. But leaving those pricey gifts at your door gives thieves a better chance of snagging them in seconds if you don’t have a plan to store them out of sight.

Sources indicate that CNET’s annual package theft survey polls US adults about their experiences with porch pirates and how they try to prevent it. This year, the average package value is close to $300, and 28% of US adults have had a package stolen, know someone who has or caught an attempted theft within the past year. Yet 20% of US adults don’t use security devices due to hardware costs or monthly subscription fees.

But leaving your packages unguarded could be a big risk — especially during the holidays. On the other hand, bad actors have been caught in the act on home security cameras. Is it really enough to deter bad actors, and what more can you do to protect your deliveries?

CNET’s findings show that some US adults have dealt with porch theft firsthand: 8% had packages meant for themselves or their households stolen within the past year, and 5% had a delivered gift stolen. Very few (1%) caught a theft in the act on a video doorbell or security camera.

Meanwhile, many US adults know someone who fell victim to package theft — 13% know a neighbor or community member who had a package stolen within the past year, and 12% know someone who doesn’t live in their community who has.

“Close to a third of our respondents are personally acquainted with package theft, which is still a high number compared to other complications like break-ins,” stated CNET’s senior home security editor, Tyler Lacoma. “Thieves generally look for crimes of opportunity, and few things are easier than a package left on a doorstep, especially if nobody is home.”.

Surprisingly, most US adults (72%) haven’t experienced package theft or know anyone who has.

Even though the percentages above may seem low, Lacoma stated that package theft typically increases during the holidays when thieves know more deliveries are likely, and upcoming porch theft tactics are always on the horizon.

There are reports of thieves trying Wi-Fi jamming to disable live security camera footage while they steal packages. And findings show that some are installing spy cams in high-value neighborhoods to learn your home’s layout and habits to take your packages shortly after they’re delivered. In recent years, pirates have even tracked shipping labels for high-value tech, like iPhones, to steal the package within minutes of arrival.

So while the majority of US adults haven’t fallen victim, that shouldn’t be a sign to shrug off the concern or relax your home security measures. Instead, now’s the time to initiative how to safely store your packages if they’re delivered while you’re away.

Online shopping and deliveries to your door can be a convenient way to check off holiday wish lists, but the average package value this holiday season is less than last year. CNET found that US adults plan to have an average of $276.24 in holiday packages delivered during this holiday season. That’s $23.82 less than last year’s average of $300.06.

By generation, Millennials also have a lower estimated average package value than last year, with an average of $227.25, compared to their 2025 package value of $307.47 — an $80.22 difference, while Gen Z’s package value is only about $7 less than last year. But any package’s value is still worth taking precautions to help prevent it from being stolen.

In a recent development, lacoma has thoughts on why that might be. In short, lower spending could mean fewer packages.

It has been revealed that “I wonder if people have also simply gotten fewer packages in general this year due to tariffs, inflation and tech prices. That could pull these numbers down,” noted Lacoma. But there’s a high chance that could be the case considering CNET’s 2026 annual holiday survey, which found that US adult tech spending is down to $808 — which is $123 less than last year’s average of $931.

Thieves may not always know what’s in boxes they’re stealing but they’re willing to take a chance. We asked US adults which items were stolen in package thefts in the past year to give you a sense of what’s at risk.

In a recent development, among the items stolen, apparel and accessories were the most common goods stolen (40%). That’s followed by toys and games (23%). Then there are everyday home basics, like decor, cookware and small appliances (19%).

In a recent development, but personal tech devices and accessories are still among the items stolen. Small accessories like phone chargers and cases are most common (16%) among tech-related packages stolen. They are followed by audio gadgets like headphones and Bluetooth speakers, along with streaming devices and soundbars (11%, respectively).

Still, more costly tech like gaming consoles (10%), computers and laptops (9%) and smart home devices (6%) are among devices stolen.

Sources indicate that you shouldn’t leave your packages up to chance. That’s why Lacoma recommends a few safer options to ensure your packages are stored securely after they’re delivered, even beyond keeping an eye on your doorbell or security camera. Instead, keep your packages out of sight with tactics like a delivery box with a code or key or ask for an in-garage delivery.

Sources indicate that “Delivery boxes have reached a fresh level of popularity in recent years as an effective way to stop porch pirates completely. However, Amazon’s Key service that delivers to your garage is an alternative,” said Lacoma. “Either way, you’ll need to trust delivery people to handle your shipments, unless you want to arrange for pickup at a nearby shipping center, which some people like to combine with other holiday errands.”.

If you don’t want to install a newly introduced security feature, try scheduling your packages to arrive when you know you’re home, requiring a signature from someone you trust or changing your delivery location to a pickup spot, like UPS’ Hold for Pick-Up locations or Amazon Lockers.

Home surveillance, like outdoor security cameras and video doorbells, can deter package thieves who don’t want to risk getting caught on camera. But US adults have mixed feelings about their effectiveness in protecting against package theft.

It has been revealed that there are two deterrents that are keeping US adults from having security devices — cost and privacy. Findings show that 20% of US adults lack home security measures due to hardware costs or monthly subscription fees. That’s followed by 9% who don’t want to use cameras because of privacy concerns.

“Fortunately, the right home security picks can solve both these problems,” remarked Lacoma. “Brands like Tapo, Eufy, Aqara and even Google Nest offer package detection and alerts for free, so you don’t have to worry about extra fees.”.

Lacoma added that many companies also offer ways to use local video storage and local AI detection so nothing is stored in the cloud. There are also features, such as customizable privacy zones, to minimize privacy concerns when used with the right precautions.

Among all US adults, only 14% have security devices with a monthly subscription that lets them save or playback video. By comparison, 12% have security devices but no subscription.

Those percentages could be low for a few reasons, including the overall perception of how helpful surveillance and security really are against porch theft. Eleven percent of US adults don’t think security devices deter porch thefts. It’s a valid concern since 4% fell victim to package theft or an attempted theft despite having security devices. And some US adults (9%) use security devices to get proof of a theft after the fact — not to prevent it.

Recent findings suggest that but that doesn’t mean you should ignore the possibility of package theft — especially during the holidays. Even if you don’t want to install cameras or new security devices, make a strategy to protect your packages and avoid the headache of package theft over the holidays.

Sources indicate that “Remember, the simple presence of a security camera is enough to make many thieves look elsewhere – interviews have confirmed it,” mentioned Lacoma. “And with today’s phone alerts about package detection, you can usually check on a package only seconds after it appears, or bring up footage if it unexpectedly vanishes, letting you take action fast. New practices like delivery boxes or in-garage delivery help address risks in concrete ways, too.”.

CNET commissioned YouGov Plc to conduct the survey. All figures, unless otherwise stated, are from YouGov Plc. The total sample size was 2,016 adults. Fieldwork was undertaken between Oct. 23–27, 2026. The survey was carried out online. The figures have been weighted and are representative of all US adults (aged 18 plus).

The $75 billion figure was calculated by multiplying the average value of deliveries each US adult expects to receive by the 2025 US population of adults ages 18 and over calculated by the US Census Bureau.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By RJ Fulton – Updated Nov 18, 2026 at 5:30AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Ford Motor Manufacturer ›.

The global automotive industry's transition toward electrification is creating new opportunities for manufacturers while challenging the profitability of established business models. For investors considering BYD (BYDDY +0.25%) and Ford Motor (F -0.12%), the two companies offer fundamentally different approaches to navigating this transition.

BYD has emerged as a global leader in electric vehicles by leveraging its vertically integrated supply chain and competitive pricing. Meanwhile, Ford continues to rely on its established truck, SUV, and commercial vehicle businesses while investing in electrification.

Although both companies face declining revenue and significant financial pressures, their contrasting business models, capital requirements, and growth prospects could make one a more attractive investment heading into 2027.

According to recent reports, with a presence in more than 120 countries, BYD is increasingly looking beyond its domestic Chinese market to drive growth. One of BYD's primary competitive advantages is its vertically integrated business model, which allows it to manufacture critical components, including batteries and semiconductors, in-house. This provides greater control over production costs and vehicle pricing.

According to recent reports, in the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached approximately $120.4 billion, representing a 4.5% year-over-year decline. Despite falling revenue, BYD generated $4.7 billion in net income, translating to a profit margin of roughly 3.9%. Maintaining profitability is particularly noteworthy given intensifying price competition in China's electric vehicle market and the costs associated with international expansion.

As of December 2025, BYD maintained a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.7 and a current ratio of 0.8. Perhaps more concerning, the tech giant recorded negative free cash flow of approximately $14.6 billion in fiscal 2025.

Recent findings suggest that ford maintains an established global automotive business supported by a network of more than 8,200 independently owned dealerships. Unlike BYD, Ford's competitive advantage stems largely from its established position in the truck, SUV, and commercial vehicle markets. Its Ford Pro division also provides fleet management, maintenance, and software services, creating revenue opportunities beyond traditional vehicle sales.

Sources indicate that in the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached approximately $187 billion, representing a 1.4% year-over-year decline. However, Ford recorded a net loss of $7.8 billion, translating to a negative profit margin of roughly 4.2%. The tech giant's deteriorating profitability highlights the challenges of maintaining its traditional automotive business while investing in electrification and navigating an increasingly competitive industry.

As of December 2025, Ford maintained a debt-to-equity ratio of 4.7 and a current ratio of 1.1. While its debt burden appears substantial, a significant portion is associated with Ford Credit, which provides financing to customers and dealerships. Additionally, Ford generated approximately $12.5 billion in free cash flow during fiscal 2025.

One of BYD's primary risks is growing trade protectionism. As the tech giant expands internationally, tariffs and restrictions on Chinese-made vehicles could undermine its pricing advantage and limit access to lucrative automotive markets. Meanwhile, intense price competition in China threatens to compress profit margins, particularly as BYD continues to allocate substantial capital to manufacturing capacity, battery technology, and overseas expansion.

Industry observers note that ford faces the challenge of balancing investments in electrification with the profitability of its traditional vehicle business. Uncertainty surrounding EV demand, government incentives, and emissions standards complicates long-term investment decisions and increases the risk of misallocating capital. Ford also remains exposed to costly vehicle recalls, warranty expenses, and rising manufacturing costs. Additionally, its reliance on truck and SUV sales makes the tech giant particularly vulnerable to weakening consumer spending and elevated borrowing costs.

Ford appears to be the more affordable option based on its lower earnings and sales multiples, which reflect the financial hurdles it currently faces.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

Ford is considerably cheaper from a valuation standpoint, trading at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 6.1 compared to BYD's 13.7. Ford also trades at just 0.2 times sales, while BYD trades at 0.6 times sales. Despite this valuation disparity, I believe BYD offers the more compelling long-term investment opportunity heading into 2027.

In a recent development, my preference for BYD comes down to the direction of the global automotive industry. As electric and hybrid vehicles become more affordable, BYD's vertically integrated business model positions it to compete aggressively on price without relying as heavily on third-party suppliers. Its diverse vehicle lineup and expanding international presence also provide multiple avenues for growth, particularly in markets where vehicle affordability remains a primary consideration for consumers.

Ford's attractive valuation and positive free cash flow shouldn't be overlooked. However, the firm faces the difficult task of protecting its traditional automotive business while developing a profitable electric vehicle operation. Although BYD's substantial cash outflows and exposure to international trade restrictions warrant caution, I believe its competitive advantages in battery technology, manufacturing efficiency, and affordable electrification justify its valuation premium over Ford.
